(6) Sūrat al-An'ām

Makkī (Meccan), except for six or three verses from His saying: "Say: Come, let me recite" (6:151 onward). It has one hundred and sixty-five verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Praise be to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth﴾. He informs that He, glory be to Him and exalted, is worthy of praise, and He draws attention to the fact that He is the one deserving of it for these great blessings, whether or not He is praised, so that it may be a proof against those who ascribe equals to their Lord. The plural "heavens" (samāwāt) is used rather than the singular, while the earth is mentioned in the singular though it is "like them," because their layers are different in essence and their effects and movements vary. He mentioned the heavens first because of their nobility, the loftiness of their place, and the priority of their existence. ﴿And made the darknesses and the light﴾: He brought them into being. The difference between "created" (khalaqa) and "made" (ja'ala), where each takes a single object, is that khalq (creating) carries the sense of determining/measuring, while ja'l (making) carries the sense of bringing something into being in a particular form. Therefore He expressed the bringing into existence of light and darkness by "making," as a reminder that they do not subsist by themselves, as the Dualists (al-Thanawiyya) claim. He used the plural "darknesses" (zulumāt) because of the multiplicity of their causes and the bodies that carry them, or because "darkness" here means misguidance and "light" means guidance; guidance is one, while misguidance is many. Its mention first is due to the precedence of privation (i'dām) over the positive attributes (malakāt).

Whoever claims that darkness is an accident that opposes light, and relies on this verse, has not known that the absence of a capacity, like blindness, is not pure non-existence, so that it would not be subject to "making." ﴿Yet those who disbelieve ascribe equals to their Lord﴾: this is coordinated with His saying "Praise be to Allah," in the sense that Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, is worthy of praise for what He created as a blessing to His servants, yet those who disbelieve in Him ascribe equals to Him, thus denying His blessing. "To their Lord" (bi-rabbihim) draws attention to the fact that He created these things as means for their existence and sustenance, so He deserves to be praised for them and not disbelieved. Alternatively, if it is coordinated with "created," the sense is that Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, created what no one other than Him can create, yet they ascribe to Him equals who have no power over anything of it. The meaning of "thumma" (yet/then) is to express the strangeness of their deviation after this explanation. The preposition "bi" in the first reading is connected to "disbelieve" and the complement of "ya'dilūn" is omitted, i.e., they turn away from Him, so that the denunciation falls on the act itself. In the second reading, it is connected to "ya'dilūn," and the meaning is that the disbelievers ascribe idols as equals to their Lord, i.e., they make them equal to Him, glory be to Him and exalted.

**Be He Who created you from clay.** That is, He began your creation from it, since it is the first material. Adam, who is the origin of humankind, was created from it. Or the meaning is "He created your father," with the noun omitted. ﴿Then He decreed a term﴾: the term of death. ﴿And a specified term with Him﴾: the term of the Resurrection. It has been said that the first term is the period between creation and death, and the second is the period between death and resurrection, since the word *ajal* (term) is used both for the end of a period and for the whole of it. It has also been said that the first term is sleep and the second is death. It has been said that the first is for those who have passed away, and the second is for those who remain and those who are yet to come. *Ajal* is an indefinite noun (*nakira*) made specific by its descriptive qualifier. For this reason the predicate was not placed first, and the sentence was begun with it, to magnify it. For this reason also it was left indefinite and described as *musamma*, meaning fixed and determined, not subject to change. Its location was described as "with God," meaning that no one else has any part in it, either by knowledge or by power. And because its clarification is the purpose of the verse.

﴿Then you doubt﴾: this is a denunciation of their doubt, after it has been established that He is their Creator, the Creator of their origins, and the One who brings them to life until their terms. For whoever is able to create the materials, gather them, place life in them, and sustain them as He wills, is even more able to gather those materials again and bring them back to life. Thus the first verse is evidence of *tawhid* (the oneness of God), and the second is evidence of *ba'th* (resurrection). *Imtira'* means doubt, and its original sense is *al-mara'*, which is extracting milk from the udder.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 3:

﴿He is Allah﴾. The pronoun refers to God, glorified and exalted be He, and "Allah" is its predicate (khabar). ﴿in the heavens and on the earth﴾ is connected to the name "Allah." The meaning is: He alone is the one deserving of worship in both of them, not another. This is like His saying, glorified and exalted be He: ﴿And He is the one who is God in the heaven, and God on the earth﴾, or like His saying: ﴿He knows your secret and your open [deeds]﴾. The clause is a second predicate, or it is the predicate and "Allah" is an apposition (badal). For the adverbial (zarfiyyah) construction to be valid, it suffices that the thing known is in both of them, like your saying "I shot the game in the sanctuary (haram)" when you were outside it while the game was inside it. Or the adverbial phrase is a settled (mustaqirr) complement that functions as the predicate, meaning that He, glorified and exalted be He, because of the completeness of His knowledge of what is in them, is as if He were in them. ﴿He knows your secret and your open [deeds]﴾ is an explanation and confirmation of this, and it is not connected to the verbal noun (masdar), because its qualifier (sifah) may not precede it. ﴿and He knows what you earn﴾ of good or evil, so He rewards for it and punishes for it. Perhaps by "the secret and the open" is meant what is hidden and what is apparent of the states of the souls, and by "what you earn" are the deeds of the limbs.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 4–5:

﴿And no sign comes to them from among the signs of their Lord﴾. Here "min" in the first instance (min āyatin) is an extra particle (ṣilah, "redundant") that conveys totality (li-l-istighrāq), while the second "min" (min āyāti) is partitive (li-l-tab'īḍ). The meaning is: no proof ever appears to them from among the proofs, or miracle from among the miracles, or sign from among the signs of the Qur'an. ﴿except that they turn away from it﴾, neglecting to reflect upon it and paying it no heed.

﴿So they have indeed denied the truth when it came to them﴾, meaning the Qur'an. This is, in effect, a consequence of what precedes it, as if it were said: since they turned away from all the signs, they denied this one when it came to them. Alternatively, it serves as evidence for that point, in the sense that since they turned away from the Qur'an and denied it, though it is the greatest of the signs, how could they not turn away from anything else? For this reason the result is introduced with the particle "fa" (so). ﴿But there will soon come to them the news of what they used to mock﴾, meaning that what they used to mock will become manifest to them when the punishment descends upon them in this world and the Hereafter, or when Islam becomes apparent and its affair is exalted.

﴿Did they not see how many generations We destroyed before them?﴾ That is, from the people of an age. A *qarn* (generation) is the span of the average lifespan of people, which is seventy years. It was also said eighty. It was also said that a *qarn* is the people of an era in which there was a prophet or someone outstanding in knowledge. The period may be short or long, and its derivation is from *qarantu* (I joined).

﴿We had established them on the earth﴾: We gave them a place in it, settled them there, and gave them of strength and means by which they could carry out various kinds of activity upon it. ﴿That which We had not established for you﴾: that which We did not grant you of ample provision and long stay, O people of Makkah, that which We did not give you of strength and abundance of wealth, and of numerical superiority and means of support. ﴿And We sent the sky upon them﴾: that is, the rain, or the clouds, or the canopy (*mizallah*); the beginning of the rain is understood from it. ﴿In abundant torrents﴾: that is, in great abundance. ﴿And We made the rivers flow beneath them﴾: so they lived in fertility and luxury, amid rivers and fruits. ﴿Then We destroyed them for their sins﴾: that is, that did not avail them anything.

﴿And We brought into being﴾: and We created. ﴿After them another generation﴾: as replacements for them. The meaning is that just as He, glorified and exalted is He, was able to destroy those before you, such as ʿAd and Thamud, and to bring into being in their place those who would populate His lands with them, so He is able to do the same to you.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 7–8:

﴿And had We sent down to you a Book on paper,﴾ written on parchment. ﴿and they had touched it with their hands,﴾ that is, they had handled it. The specification of touching is because forgery does not occur in it, so they could not say, "Our eyes have only been dazzled." And because sight precedes it, where there is no obstacle. Its restriction to the hands is to remove the metaphorical sense, for it may be used metaphorically for investigation, as in His saying: "And we have touched the heaven." ﴿those who disbelieved would have said, "This is nothing but obvious magic."﴾ out of obstinacy and stubbornness.

﴿And they say, "Why was not an angel sent down to him?"﴾ Why was an angel not sent down with him, speaking to us that he is a prophet, as in His saying: ﴿"Why was there not sent down to him an angel so that he would be with him a warner?"﴾ ﴿And had We sent down an angel, the matter would have been decided,﴾ this is a reply to their saying and an explanation of what prevents what they proposed and of the flaw in it. The meaning is that if an angel were sent down in a manner in which they could see him, as they proposed, their destruction would be certain, for God's way has run this way with those before them. ﴿Then they would not be reprieved﴾ for a moment after his descent.

"And if We had made him an angel, We would have made him a man, and We would have confused them as they confuse themselves." This is a second response, if the pronoun refers to the one sought (the sought-after sign); and if it refers to the Messenger, then it is a second answer to their demand, for they sometimes say, "Why was an angel not sent down to him?" and at other times say, "If our Lord willed, He would have sent down angels."

The meaning is: if We had made a companion for you an angel whom they could see, or made the Messenger an angel, We would have given him the form of a man, just as Gabriel was made to appear in the form of Dihya al-Kalbi, for human strength cannot withstand seeing the angel in his own form. It is also read as "lalabasna" with a single lam, and as "lallabbasna" with shaddah, for emphasis.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 10–11:

﴿And indeed, messengers before you were mocked﴾ as a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for what he sees from his people. ﴿So there befell those who mocked them, of them, what they used to mock at﴾: what they used to mock at encompassed them, since they were destroyed on account of it; or the consequence of their mockery came down upon them.

﴿Say: "Travel through the earth, then observe how was the end of those who denied"﴾: how Allah destroyed them with the punishment of annihilation, so that you may take heed. The difference between this and His saying: ﴿Say: "Travel through the earth and observe"﴾ is that travel there is for the sake of observation, whereas here it is not so; therefore it has been said that its meaning is the permissibility of travel for trade and other purposes, and the obligation to observe the traces of those who perished.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 12–13:

﴿Say: To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth?﴾ — in terms of creation and dominion. This is a question of rebuke. ﴿Say: To Allah.﴾ — as an affirmation to them and an alert that He is the one who is definitively the answer, such that they cannot mention anyone other than Him. ﴿He has prescribed for Himself mercy.﴾ — He bound Himself to it out of bounty and beneficence. By mercy is meant what encompasses both abodes, and among it is guidance to the knowledge of Him, knowledge of His oneness through the establishment of proofs, the sending down of Books, and granting respite to disbelief. ﴿He will surely gather you unto the Day of Resurrection.﴾ — this is a resumptive statement and an oath, a threat for their associating partners with Him and their heedlessness (p-156) of reflection; that is: He will surely gather you in the graves, raised up until the Day of Resurrection, and then He will recompense you for your polytheism. Or: on the Day of Resurrection, with ilá (to) meaning fī (in). It was said that it is a partial substitute (badal al-ba'd) for mercy, for among His mercy is His resurrecting you and His favour upon you. ﴿There is no doubt concerning it.﴾ — concerning the Day or the gathering. ﴿Those who have lost their souls.﴾ — by squandering their capital, which is the innate disposition (fitrah) and sound reason. The position of alladhīna (those who) is in the accusative case by way of dispraise, or in the nominative case as the predicate, meaning: "and you are those who," or it is in the nominative as the subject with a predicate. ﴿So they do not believe.﴾ — the fā' indicates that their non-belief is caused by their loss; for nullifying reason through following the senses and imagination, immersion in imitation (taqlid), and heedlessness of reflection led them to persist in disbelief and to refrain from faith. ﴿And to Him belongs﴾ — a conjunction upon li-Llāh (to Allah). ﴿whatever dwells in the night and the day.﴾ — from sukna (dwelling), with its transitive particle fī as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you dwelt in the dwellings of those who wronged themselves﴾; the meaning is what the two comprise. Or it is from sukūn (stillness), meaning what is still and moves within them, and it suffices with one of the two opposites over the other. ﴿And He is the All-Hearing﴾ — of every thing heard. ﴿the All-Knowing﴾ — of every thing known, so nothing is hidden from Him. It is also permissible that this be a threat to the polytheists regarding their sayings and their deeds.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 14:

﴿Say: "Shall I take as a protector other than Allah?"﴾ This is a denial of taking other than Allah as a protector, not a denial of taking a protector. Therefore the interrogative particle (hamzah) has been placed first and has been given precedence. The meaning of "protector" here is the one worshipped, because this is a rebuttal to those who invited him to association (shirk). ﴿Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾: the one who brought them into being. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him: "I did not know the meaning of al-Fatir (the Originator) until two Bedouins came to me disputing over a well, and one of them said, 'I am the one who fathartuha (originated it),' meaning I began it." It is in the genitive as an attributive adjective of Allah, since it carries the meaning of the past tense. For this reason it was read as "fuțira" (in the passive). It was also read in the nominative and accusative, as a laudatory epithet (madh).

﴿And He feeds but is not fed﴾: He provides sustenance and is not provided for. The specification of food is due to the intensity of the need for it. It was read as "wa la yut'am" (with a fatha on the ya'), and with the reverse of the first (i.e., the verb is passive for the first and active for the second), on the basis that the pronoun refers to other than Allah, and the meaning is: how can I associate with one who is the Originator of the heavens and the earth, when that which I would worship has fallen from the rank of living beings? It was also read with both verbs in the active form, on the basis that the second is from aṭ'ama in the sense of istaṭ'ama (to ask for food), or on the meaning that He feeds at times and does not feed at other times, like His saying: ﴿He grasps and extends﴾ (2:245). ﴿Say: "I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit"﴾, because the Prophet ﷺ precedes his community in religion. ﴿And do not be among the polytheists﴾. It has been said that this was addressed to me, and "wa la takunanna" (do not be) is a continuation of the command "Say"; it is also permissible for it to be coordinated with "Say."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 15–16:

﴿Say: Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord, the punishment of a great day.﴾ This is another emphatic measure for cutting off their hopes, and an allusion to them that they are sinners deserving of punishment. The conditional clause is interposed between the verb and its object, and its response is omitted, indicated by the sentence that precedes it.

﴿Whoever is turned away from it on that day﴾ meaning: the punishment is turned away from him. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ya'qub, and Abu Bakr (on the authority of 'Asim) read "yuṣraf" (is turned away) with the pronoun referring to God, glorified and exalted be He. It has also been read with the pronoun made explicit, and the object is then omitted; or "yawma'idhin" is read with the noun governed by an elided genitive construction (i.e., the punishment of that day). ﴿Then indeed He has had mercy on him﴾ meaning: He has saved him and bestowed favor upon him. ﴿And that is the clear triumph﴾ meaning: that turning away or that mercy.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 19:

﴿Say: "What thing is greatest in testimony?"﴾ It was revealed when the Quraysh said: "O Muhammad, we asked the Jews and the Christians about you, and they claimed that there is no mention or description of you among them. So show us someone who will testify that you are the Messenger of God." The word "thing" (shay') applies to every existing thing, and the discussion of it has already preceded in surah al-Baqarah. ﴿Say: "God"﴾, meaning: God is the greatest in testimony. Then he begins: ﴿He is a witness between me and you﴾, meaning: He is a witness between me and you. It is also permissible that "God is a witness" is the answer, because when He, glorified and exalted is He, is the Witness, He is the greatest thing in testimony. ﴿And this Qur'an has been revealed to me that I may warn you thereby﴾, meaning: with the Qur'an. He suffices with mention of warning instead of mention of good tidings. ﴿And whomever it reaches﴾ is conjoined to the pronoun of those addressed, meaning: that I may warn you thereby, O people of Makkah, and all others it reaches of the black and the red, or of the two weighty things (humans and jinn), or: that I may warn you thereby, you who exist, and whoever it reaches until the Day of Resurrection. In this is evidence that the rulings of the Qur'an encompass those present at the time of its revelation and those after them, and that one is not held accountable for them if it has not reached him. ﴿Do you indeed testify that there are other gods along with God?﴾ is a confirmation to them together with denial and disapproval. ﴿Say: "I do not testify"﴾ to what you testify. ﴿Say: "He is only one God"﴾, meaning: rather, I testify that there is no god but Him. ﴿And indeed I am free from what you associate﴾, meaning: the idols.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 20–21:

﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognise him﴾ they recognise the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) by his description mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel. ﴿as they recognise their own sons﴾ by their features. ﴿Those who have lost their souls﴾ from among the People of the Book and the polytheists. ﴿they do not believe﴾ because they have squandered that by which faith is acquired.

﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah,﴾ like their saying: the angels are the daughters of Allah, and these are our intercessors with Allah. ﴿or denies His signs?﴾ like their denying the Qur'an and the miracles and calling them magic. The use of "or" here, when they have combined both matters, is to draw attention to the fact that each of the two on its own reaches the utmost extreme of wrongdoing against oneself. ﴿Indeed, He﴾ the pronoun refers to the matter (al-sha'n, the "it" of the situation). ﴿the wrongdoers will not prosper﴾ let alone those than whom none is more unjust.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 22–23:

﴿And the Day We gather them all together﴾ is in the accusative, governed by a suppressed verb, to magnify the matter (tahwil lil-amr). ﴿Then We will say to those who associated partners [with God]: "Where are your partners,"﴾ that is, your gods which you made partners with God. Ya'qub read «yahshuruhum» and «yaqulu» with the letter ya' (in the third person). ﴿whom you used to claim﴾ that is, you used to claim them to be partners. Both objects have been omitted, and the purpose of the interrogation is rebuke (tawbikh). Perhaps they will be made to be separated from their gods at that time, so that they lose them at the very hour in which they had placed their hope. It is also possible that they will see them, but since [the gods] did not benefit them, it is as if they were absent from them.

﴿Then their fitnah will be nothing but that they will say﴾ that is, their disbelief (kufr), and what is meant is its consequence. It is also said that it means their excuse, by which they imagine they will be delivered, from "fatantu al-dhahab" when one refines gold. It is also said that it means their answer. He called it fitnah because it is a lie, or because they intended by it deliverance.

Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Hafs from 'Asim read «lam takun» with the letter ta' and «fitnatuhum» in the nominative, on the basis that it is the subject (ism). Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr (from him) read it with the ta' and in the accusative, on the basis that the subject is «an qalu», and the feminine marking is for the predicate, like their saying "man kanat ummuka" (who is your mother). The rest read it with the ya' and in the accusative. ﴿By God, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ they lie and swear upon it, while knowing that it will not benefit them, out of extreme bewilderment and astonishment, just as they say: "Our Lord, bring us out of it" (rabbana akhrijna minha). They had already been certain of eternal abiding. It is also said that its meaning is: "We were not polytheists in our own estimation," but this does not agree with His saying.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 24–25:

﴿Look how they lied against themselves﴾, i.e., by denying association (shirk) with Him. Taking it to mean their lying in this world is a forced interpretation (ta'assuf) that disrupts the composition (nuzm). A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿On the day when Allah raises them all up, and they swear to Him as they swear to you﴾. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "rabbana" (﴿our Lord﴾) in the accusative case, as a vocative (nida') or as a laudatory address (madh). ﴿And what they used to invent has forsaken them﴾, namely the partners.

﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ when you recite the Qur'an. The intended ones are Abu Sufyan, al-Walid, al-Nadr, Utbah, Shaybah, Abu Jahl and their like. They gathered and heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reciting the Qur'an, so they said to al-Nadr, "What is he saying?" He said, "By the One who made it (the Ka'bah) His house, I do not know what he is saying, except that he moves his tongue and says, 'the fables of the ancients,' just as I have related to you about the past generations." Abu Sufyan said, "I indeed see that it is true." Abu Jahl said, "No!" ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings (akinnah)﴾, i.e., veils, the plural of kinan, which is that which conceals a thing. ﴿So that they do not understand it (an yafqahuhu)﴾, meaning out of aversion to their understanding it. ﴿And in their ears is deafness (waqr)﴾, which prevents them from hearing it. The verification of this has already been discussed at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

﴿And if they see every sign, they will not believe in it﴾, due to their extreme obstinacy and the firmly rooted imitation (taqlid) among them. ﴿Until, when they come to you disputing with you﴾, i.e., their denial of the signs reached the point that they came to you disputing with you. "Hatta" here is the one after which sentences occur, having no governing effect (amal). The clause, "when" (idha) and its answer, which is: ﴿those who disbelieved say, "This is nothing but the fables of the ancients"﴾, makes their making the most truthful speech into the myths of the ancients the utmost extent of denial. "Yujadiluna-naka" is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to their coming. It is also permissible for "hatta" to be the preposition (jarrah), with "idha ja'uka" in the position of a genitive, "yujadiluna-naka" a circumstantial clause, and "yaqulu" an explanation of it. "Al-asatir" means the falsehoods, the plural of "usturah" or "isharah" or "asfar," the plural of "satr," whose origin is "al-satr" in the sense of a line.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 6, verses 26–27:

﴿And they forbid others from it⦆ That is, they forbid people from the Qur'an, or from the Messenger ﷺ and from believing in him. ﴿And they keep away from it⦆ by themselves, or they forbid people from harming the Messenger of God ﷺ, and they keep away from him, so they do not believe in him, like Abu Talib. ﴿And they destroy none but themselves⦆ and they do not destroy anyone by that. ﴿Yet they are unaware⦆ that its harm does not extend beyond them to others.

﴿If only you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire⦆ Its response (jawab) is omitted, meaning: if only you could see them when they are brought to ﴿the Fire⦆ so that they witness it, or look down upon it, or enter it and thereby know the extent of its punishment, you would see a dreadful matter. It is also read as "waqafu" (they were made to stand), in the active form, from "waqafa 'alayha wuqufan" (he stood over it). ﴿Then they will say: "Would that we were returned!"⦆ expressing a wish (tamanni) to return to the world. ﴿And not deny the signs of our Lord, and be among the believers⦆ is a resumed speech (isti'naf) from them, in the affirmative sense, like their saying: "Leave me, and I will not return," meaning: "And I will not return, even if you left me or did not leave me." Or it is conjoined (ʿatf) to "we would be returned," or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in it, in which case it has the status of a wish. Their words ﴿and indeed they are liars⦆ refer back to what the wish contains of a promise. Hamzah, Ya'qub and Hafs read both verbs in the subjunctive, as a response (jawab), by implying "an" after the "wa" (and), treating it as if it had the place of the "fa" (then). Ibn 'Amir read the first in the nominative, as a conjunction (ʿatf), and the second in the subjunctive, as a response.(p-159)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 28–29:

﴿Nay, there has become apparent to them what they used to conceal before﴾. This is a turning away (idrab) from the will to believe that is understood from their wish (tamanni). The meaning is that there became apparent to them what they used to conceal of their hypocrisy, or the ugly nature of their deeds; so they wished for that out of distress, not with a firm resolve that, had they been returned, they would have believed.

﴿And had they been returned﴾, i.e., to the world after standing (before the Fire) and witnessing its reality. ﴿They would surely have returned to what they were forbidden﴾ of disbelief and disobedience. ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾ in what they promised of themselves.

﴿And they said﴾ is either a conjunction (atf) upon "they would have returned" (la'adu), or upon "indeed they are liars" (innahum lakadhibun), or upon "were forbidden" (nuhu); or it is a resumption (isti'naf), mentioning what they said in the world.

﴿There is only our life of this world﴾, the pronoun (hiya) refers to "life" (hayah), ﴿and we are not to be resurrected﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 30–31:

﴿And if you could see when they are made to stand before their Lord﴾ is a metaphor for being detained for questioning and rebuke. It has also been said that its meaning is: they are made to stand before the decree of their Lord or His recompense, or they came to know Him with the fullest knowledge.

﴿He will say: Is this not the truth?﴾ It is as if a questioner asks: what did their Lord say at that time?

The interrogative particle (hamza) here is for reproach over their denial, and the reference is to the Resurrection and what follows it of reward and punishment. ﴿They will say: Yes, by our Lord!﴾ is a emphatic affirmation with an oath, so that the matter becomes entirely clear. ﴿He will say: Taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve﴾ because of your disbelief, or in exchange for it.

﴿Those who denied the meeting with Allah have certainly lost﴾ for the bliss has escaped them and they have merited the lasting punishment. The meeting with Allah is the Resurrection and what follows it.

﴿Until, when the Hour comes upon them suddenly﴾ is the limit (ghayah) for "denied," not for "lost," because their loss has no limit. ﴿Suddenly﴾ means unexpectedly, and its accusative form is either as a circumstantial state (hal) or as a verbal noun (masdar), since it is a kind of coming. ﴿They will say: Oh, our regret!﴾ meaning: "Come, for this is your time." ﴿For what we neglected concerning it﴾ meaning we fell short regarding it in the worldly life. The object is left implied, though it has not been mentioned, because it is known; or it refers to the Hour, meaning regarding its matter and belief in it.

﴿And they will carry their burdens upon their backs﴾ is an image of their deserving the heavy loads of sins. ﴿Unquestionably, evil is what they carry﴾ meaning: wretched is the thing they bear as their burden.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 32:

﴿And the life of this world is nothing but play and amusement﴾ meaning: its deeds are nothing but play and amusement, which divert people and occupy them from what yields lasting benefit and true pleasure. This is a response to their saying: ﴿There is naught but our life of this world﴾.

﴿And the Last Abode is better for those who fear God﴾ because of its permanence and the purity of its benefits and pleasures. His saying ﴿for those who fear God﴾ is a reminder that what is not among the deeds of the God-fearing is play and amusement. Ibn 'Amir recited it as «wa-la-dar al-akhirah» (wa-la-dāru l-ākhirah).

﴿Will you not then use your reason?﴾ meaning: which of the two is better? Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hafs from 'Asim, and Ya'qub recited it with the letter "ta'" (taʿqilūna, "will you not reason?"), addressing those being spoken to, or giving precedence to the present over the absent.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 33:

﴿We know indeed that what they say grieves you﴾. The meaning of qad (indeed) here is the emphasis of the verb and its frequency, as in his saying:

"But indeed, its recipient may destroy the wealth" (wa-lakinnahu qad yuhliku al-mala na'iluh).

The ha' in innahu (that it) refers to the matter (al-sha'n, the dummy pronoun). It is also read as "layuhzinuka" from ahzana (to grieve, in causative form). ﴿Yet they do not deny you﴾ in reality. Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read "la yukadhdhibunaka" from akdhabahu (to find someone a liar), or (to attribute lying to him). ﴿But it is the wrongdoers who deny the signs of God﴾: that is, they deny and reject the signs of God. The expression "the wrongdoers" is placed in the position of the pronoun to indicate that they did wrong by their denial, or that they denied out of habituation to wrongdoing. The ba' (bi) is there because juhud (denial) is used in the sense of takdhib (rejecting as false).

It is narrated that Abu Jahl used to say: "We do not deny you, for you are truthful in our eyes, but we deny what you have brought to us." So this verse was revealed.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 34:

﴿Indeed, messengers were denied before you﴾ as a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). In this there is evidence that His saying "they do not deny you" (6:33) does not negate their denial of him absolutely. ﴿So they were patient over being denied and harmed﴾ over their denial and their harming of them; so take them as an example (tasa​ssi bihim) and be patient. ﴿Until Our help came to them﴾ contains an allusion to the promise of help for those who are patient. ﴿And there is none to alter the words of Allah﴾ i.e., His promises, from His saying: ﴿And Our word had already preceded to Our servants, the messengers﴾ (37:171) and so on. ﴿And there has certainly come to you some of the news of the messengers﴾ i.e., some of their stories and what they endured from their peoples.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 35:

﴿And if their turning away is grievous to you﴾: it is great and burdensome, [namely] their aversion from you and from belief in what you have brought. ﴿So if you are able to seek a tunnel in the earth or a ladder into the sky and bring them a sign﴾: a passage by which you could penetrate into the depths of the earth and bring forth for them a sign, or a means of ascent by which you could climb into the sky and bring down from it a sign. "In the earth" is a qualifier of "tunnel" (nafaqan), and "in the sky" is a qualifier of "ladder" (sullaman). It is permissible that both be dependent on "seek" (tabtaghi), or that they be two circumstantial clauses (hal) from the pronoun concealed within it. The second conditional's answer (jawab al-shart al-thani) is omitted, its estimate being "then do it," and the clause is the answer to the first. The purpose is to show his intense eagerness for the Islam of his people, and that, had he been able to bring them a sign from beneath the earth or from above the sky, he would have brought it, hoping for their faith. ﴿And if God had willed, He would have gathered them upon guidance﴾: that is, if God had willed to gather them upon guidance, He would have granted them success in belief until they believed, but His will was not related to this, so do not be consumed over it. The Mu'tazilah interpreted it as meaning that had He willed to gather them upon guidance, by bringing them a compelling sign, but He did not do so, since that would depart from wisdom. ﴿So do not be among the ignorant﴾: [by being] greedy for what will not happen, and impatient in situations that call for patience, for that is the practice of the ignorant.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 36–37:

﴿Only those who listen will respond﴾ Only those who listen with understanding and reflection will respond, referring to His words: ﴿Or he who gives ear while he is a witness﴾. These are like the dead who do not hear. ﴿And the dead—Allah will raise them﴾, so He will inform them when faith will no longer benefit them. ﴿Then to Him they will be returned﴾ for recompense.

(p-161) ﴿And there is no creature moving on the earth⦆ walking upon its surface. ﴿Nor a bird that flies with its two wings⦆ in the air; he described it thus to exclude the metaphorical sense of speed and the like. It is also read "wa-lā ṭā'irun" (nor a bird) in the nominative, on the basis of the place (maḥall). ﴿But they are communities like you⦆ whose conditions are preserved and whose provisions and terms (ājāl) are decreed. The purpose of this is to indicate the perfection of His power, the comprehensiveness of His knowledge and the breadth of His governance, so that it serves as evidence that He is able to send down a sign (āyah). The plural "umam" (communities) is used in view of the meaning. ﴿We have not neglected anything in the Book⦆ meaning the Preserved Tablet (al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ), for it comprises what occurs in the world, both the great and the minute, and no matter concerning any animal or inanimate thing has been neglected in it. Here "min" is extra (mazīdah) and "shay'" stands in the position of the verbal noun (maṣdar), not the direct object, since faraṭa does not take a direct object by itself, and it has been construed with "fī" to "al-Kitāb." Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 39:

﴿And those who deny Our signs are deaf and dumb﴾: they do not hear such signs as these, which indicate His lordship, the perfection of His knowledge, and the greatness of His power, with a hearing by which their souls are affected. ﴿And dumb﴾: they do not speak the truth. ﴿In darknesses﴾: a third predicate, meaning they are groping about in the darknesses of disbelief (kufr), or in the darkness of ignorance, the darkness of obstinacy, and the darkness of blind imitation (taqlid). It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun concealed in the predicate. ﴿Whomever Allah wills, He leads astray﴾: whomever Allah wills to lead astray, He leads astray. This is a clear proof for us against the Mu'tazilah. ﴿And whomever He wills, He places on a straight path﴾: by guiding him to guidance and bringing him to it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 40–41:

﴿Say: "Tell me, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you, would you call upon other than Allah, if you are truthful?"﴾ The interrogative here is one of amazement (istifham ta'jib). The kaf (ك) is a particle of address (harf khitab), used to emphasise the pronoun (li-l-ta'kid); it has no place in i'rab (grammatical case-analysis), because you say: "Ara'aytuka Zaydan ma sha'nuh" (Tell me about yourself, Zayd: what is his affair?). If the kaf were a direct object, as the Kufans held, the verb would be transitive to three objects, and the verse would then have to read "Ara'aytumuka" (with the pronoun of the second person plural attached to it). Rather, the verb is suspended (mu'allaq), or the object is omitted, its estimated form being: "Ara'aytukum alihatakum tanfa'ukum, idh tad'unaha" (Tell me, your gods, will they benefit you, when you call upon them?). Nafi' recited "ara'aytukum," "ara'ayt," "ara'aytum," "afara'aytum," "afara'ayta" and the like, when a hamza preceded the rā', with the softening (tashil) of the hamza that follows the rā'. Al-Kisa'i omitted it altogether, and the rest recited it fully (tahqiq). Hamzah, when pausing, agreed with Nafi'. ﴿If the punishment of Allah comes upon you﴾ as it came upon those before you. ﴿Or the Hour comes upon you﴾, and he is its (the Hour's) subject, and this indicates it. ﴿Would you call upon other than Allah﴾, and this is a rebuke for them. ﴿If you are truthful﴾ that the idols are gods; its answer is omitted, meaning: then call upon Him.

﴿Rather, it is Him you call upon﴾: rather, you single Him out for supplication, as is related of them in several places. The fronting of the object serves to convey exclusivity (takhsis).

﴿So He removes that for which you call upon Him﴾: that is, what you call upon Him to remove. ﴿If He wills﴾: that is, He bestows His favour upon you, and He does not will it in the Hereafter.

﴿And you forget what you associate﴾: and you abandon your gods at that time, because of what is fixed in the intellects that He alone is able to remove harm, apart from anyone else. Or: and you forget Him because of the severity and terror of the matter.

"And We certainly sent [messengers] to communities before you (qablika), i.e., before you, and min is extra (za'ida). Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 44–45:

﴿So when they forgot what they had been reminded of﴾ (of the hardship and adversity), and did not take heed from it. ﴿We opened for them the gates of everything﴾ of kinds of blessings, alternating them between the two states of adversity and ease, and as a trial for them through hardship and prosperity, to establish the proof against them and remove any excuse, or as a deception against them, according to what is narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "A deception against the people, by the Lord of the Ka'bah."

And Ibn 'Amir read "fatahna" with the doubled letter (tashdid) throughout the Qur'an, and Ya'qub agreed with him in everything except this one and the one in "al-A'raf."

﴿Until, when they rejoiced﴾ (were pleased) ﴿in what they had been given﴾ of blessings, and they increased in nothing but insolence and being preoccupied with the blessings rather than the Benefactor, and not fulfilling His right, glorified and exalted is He. ﴿Then We seized them suddenly, and at once they were in despair﴾ (grieving and hopeless).

﴿And We send not the messengers except as bringers of good news﴾ to the believers of the Garden, ﴿and warners﴾ to the disbelievers of the Fire. We did not send them so that they would propose [demands] to them and amuse themselves with them. ﴿So whoever believes and makes amends﴾ with what must be amended, in accordance with what He has legislated for them, ﴿there is no fear for them﴾ of punishment, ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾ over the loss of reward.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 50–51:

﴿Say: I do not tell you that with me are the treasuries of Allah﴾, i.e., His decrees (maqdurat) or the treasuries of His provision. ﴿Nor do I know the unseen﴾, i.e., what has not been revealed to me and for which no proof has been established; and this is part of what is to be said. ﴿Nor do I tell you that I am an angel﴾, i.e., of the kind of the angels, or that I have power over what they have power over. ﴿I only follow what is revealed to me﴾: he disavows the claim to divinity and to angelhood, and claims prophethood (nubuwwah), which is among the perfections of humankind, in response to their deeming his claim far-fetched and their certainty that his claim is false. ﴿Say: Are the blind and the seeing equal?﴾ This is an example for the misguided and the guided, or for the ignorant and the knowing, or for one who claims the impossible, such as divinity and angelhood, and one who claims the upright, such as prophethood.

﴿Will you not then reflect?﴾ So that you may be guided, or so that you may distinguish between the claim to truth and the claim to falsehood, or so that you may know that following revelation is something from which there is no escape.

﴿And warn with it﴾: the pronoun refers to what is revealed to me. ﴿Those who fear that they will be gathered to their Lord﴾: they are the believers who fall short in action, or those who consider the gathering possible, whether they are believers or unbelievers, acknowledging it or doubting it, for warning is effective among them, unlike the idle and the resolute who are certain of its impossibility. ﴿For them there will be no protector or intercessor apart from Him﴾: this is in a position of circumstantial clause (hal) relative to "yuhsharu," for what is feared is the gathering in this state. ﴿That they may be wary (la'allahum yattaqun)﴾: i.e., in order that they may fear God.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 52:

﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾ after He had commanded him to warn those who do not fear God so that they would fear His command, and (commanded him) to honour the God-fearing, bring them close, and not drive them away, in order to please the Quraysh.

It is related that they said: "If you drive away these slaves," meaning the poor Muslims such as Ammar, Suhayb, Khabbab and Salman, "we will sit with you and converse with you." He said: "I am not one to drive away the believers." They said: "Then remove them from us when we come to you." He said: "Yes."

It is also related that Umar, may God be pleased with him, said to him: "If you did so, (it would be) until we see what they will become." So he called for the document and for Ali, may God Most High be pleased with him, to write it, and then (the verse) was revealed.

The mention of "morning and evening" is meant to indicate constancy. It has been said that it refers to the two prayers of dawn and afternoon.

Ibn Amir read بِالغَدْوَةِ here and in al-Kahf.

﴿seeking His face﴾ is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative, a word describing the state of the subject at the time of the action) of يَدْعُونَ, meaning: they call upon their Lord sincere in it. He made the restriction of the supplication to sincerity explicit, as an alert that this is the essence of the matter. He linked the prohibition to it, indicating that it requires honouring them and is incompatible with distancing them.

﴿Upon you is nothing of their reckoning, and upon them nothing of your reckoning﴾: that is, the reckoning of their faith is not incumbent on you. Perhaps their faith with God is greater than the faith of those whom you would drive away, by asking them (to leave), in hope of their faith should they believe. Or: it is not incumbent on you to consider their inner states and sincerity, since they have adopted the conduct of the God-fearing, even if they have an inner state that is not pleasing, as the polytheists mentioned and as they slandered their religion. Their reckoning is upon them and does not extend to you, just as your reckoning is upon you and does not extend to them.

It has been said: "Upon you is nothing of the reckoning of their provision," that is, of their poverty. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the polytheists, and the meaning is: you will not be held to account for them, nor they for you, so that you would be concerned about their faith to the point that you drive away the believers in hope of it.

﴿so that you would drive them away﴾: فَتَطْرُدَهُمْ means "so that you would distance them," and it is the answer (jawāb) to the negation. ﴿and you would be among the wrongdoers﴾ is the answer to the prohibition. It is permissible to conjoin فَتَطْرُدَهم (with فَتَكُونَ) on the basis of causation (tasabbub, the sense that one thing results from another), but there is scrutiny in this.

(p-164) ﴿And thus We tried some of them by means of others﴾: likewise are trials (fitan), namely the differences in people's circumstances concerning worldly affairs. "We tried" means: We tested some of them by means of others in matters of religion, when We advanced these weak ones over the nobles of Quraysh by their precedence in accepting faith. ﴿So that they say: "Are these the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favour from among us?"﴾ That is: "Are these the ones whom Allah has favoured with guidance and success in what makes them happy, rather than us, while we are the great ones and the leaders and they are the poor and the weak?" This is a denial that these people should be singled out from among them for reaching the truth and being foremost in good, as in their saying: "Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it." The lam (ل) is for consequence (al-'aqibah) or for causation (al-ta'lil), on the basis that "We tried" includes the meaning of "We abandoned" (khadhalna). ﴿Is not Allah most knowing of those who are grateful?﴾ Of those from whom faith and gratitude proceed, so He grants them success, and of those from whom they do not proceed, so He forsakes them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 54:

﴿When those who believe in Our signs come to you, say: "Peace be upon you. Your Lord has prescribed for Himself mercy."﴾ Those who believe (alladhina yu'minun) are those who call upon their Lord. He described them with belief in the Qur'an and following the proofs, after describing them with their constancy in worship, and He commanded him to begin with the greeting (al-taslim) or to convey God Almighty's greeting to them, and to give them the good news of the vastness of God Almighty's mercy and bounty, after the prohibition against driving them away. This is a notice that they are those who combine the two virtues of knowledge and action, and whoever is like this should be brought near and not driven away, honored and not humiliated, and given good news from God of safety in this world and mercy in the Hereafter.

It was said: "A people came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'Indeed we have committed great sins,' and he did not return anything to them, so they departed, and then this was revealed."

﴿that whoever among you does evil in ignorance⦆ is a resumptive clause explaining the mercy. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and Ya'qub read it with a fatha, as a substitute (badal) for it. ﴿in ignorance⦆ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: whoever commits a sin while ignorant of the reality of the harms and corruptions that follow from it, like 'Umar in what he indicated, or one who is characterized by the act of ignorance, for committing what leads to harm is among the deeds of the foolish and ignorant. ﴿then repents after it⦆ after the deed or the evil. ﴿and makes amends⦆ by remedying and resolving not to return to it. ﴿indeed He is Forgiving, Merciful⦆: its being fathah, differing from the first, is read by all except Nafi', on the supposition of an omitted subject or predicate, meaning: his matter is (that) or for him is His forgiveness.

And thus (ﷺ)... [translation follows]

Here is the translation:

"And thus" — that is, in the same manner as this clear detailing. "We detail the signs" — that is, the verses of the Qur'an, concerning the description of the obedient and of the criminals who persist in their crime, and of those who turn back (to God in repentance). "That the way of the criminals may become clear" — Nafi' read it with the ta' (tā', "that... may become clear"; the verb in the second person) and put the word "way" (sabīl) in the accusative, meaning: "and that you, O Muhammad, may make clear their way, so that you deal with each of them according to what is due to him; thus We have detailed this detailing." Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Ya'qub, and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim read it with the raf' (nominative) on the sense: "and that We may make clear their way." The rest read it with the ya' (yā', "that... may become clear," the verb in the third person masculine) and the raf', taking the word "way" (sabīl) as masculine, since sabīl may be both masculine and feminine. It is also permissible for it to be coordinated (ʿaṭf) with an implied cause (ʿillah muqaddarah), meaning: "We detail the signs so that the truth may appear, and so that it may become clear."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 56:

﴿Say: Indeed, I have been forbidden﴾ I have been turned away and restrained by the proofs that were set up for me and the signs that were sent down to me concerning the matter of tawhid (monotheism). ﴿to worship those whom you invoke besides Allah﴾ meaning, to refrain from worshipping what you worship besides Allah, or what you call gods, that is, what you name them. ﴿Say: I will not follow your desires﴾ This is an emphasis to cut off their hopes, and an indication of the reason that requires the prohibition and the cause for abstaining from following them; it is also a rebuke to them for their ignorance, and an explanation of the root of their misguidance, namely that what they hold to is desire and not guidance, and an admonition to whoever seeks the truth that he should follow the proof and not merely imitate. ﴿Then I would have gone astray﴾ that is, if I followed your desires, then I would have indeed gone astray. ﴿and I would not be among the guided﴾ that is, I would not be guided in any respect so as to be counted among them; and in this there is an implicit allusion that they are likewise.(p-165)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 57–58:

﴿Say: "Indeed, I am upon clear evidence from my Lord"﴾ This is an alert to what must be followed, after he had explained what must not be followed. Al-bayyinah (clear evidence) is the manifest proof that distinguishes truth from falsehood. It is said that what is meant by it is the Qur'an and revelation, or rational arguments, or what encompasses them. ﴿from my Lord﴾ [means] from knowledge of Him and that there is no deity besides Him. It is permissible for it to be an attribute of bayyinah. ﴿And you have denied it﴾: the pronoun refers to my Lord, meaning you have denied Him in that you associated others with Him; or it refers to bayyinah according to its meaning. ﴿What you are hastening for is not with me﴾, meaning the punishment that they sought to hasten by their saying:

﴿"Rain down upon us stones from the sky, or bring us a painful punishment."﴾ ﴿Judgment belongs only to Allah﴾ regarding the hastening of the punishment and its delay.

He decides the truth, i.e., He judges the true judgment; or He manages and arranges the truth, from their saying "qadha al-dir'a" (he fashioned the coat of mail) when he made it, concerning what He decides of hastening and delaying. The origin of qada' (judgment/decree) is decisive settlement upon the completion of a matter, and the origin of hukm (ruling) is prevention, as if He prevents falsehood. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and 'Asim read ﴿yaqussu﴾ (He relates), from qassa al-athar (he tracked the trail), or from qassa al-khabar (he related the report). ﴿And He is the best of deciders﴾, i.e., the best of judges.

﴿Say: "If what you are hastening for were with me"﴾, i.e., within my power and capacity, ﴿the punishment you seek to hasten﴾, ﴿the matter would have been decided between me and you﴾: I would have destroyed you immediately, in anger for my Lord, and what is between me and you would have ended. ﴿And Allah is most knowing of the wrongdoers﴾: in the sense of a qualification (istidrak), as if he said: "But the matter is with Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and He is most knowing of whom it is fitting to seize and whom it is fitting to give respite among them."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 59:

﴿And with Him are the keys of the unseen (mafatih al-ghayb)﴾ Its treasures. It is the plural of maftah, with a fatha on the mim, meaning a treasury, or that by which one reaches the unseen things. It is a metaphor taken from the maftah (keys), which is the plural of miftah with a kasra on the mim, meaning the key. This is supported by the reading "mafatih" (with ya'), and the meaning is that He is the one who reaches the unseen things, whose knowledge encompasses them.
﴿None knows them but He﴾ So He knows their times, and what wisdom lies in hastening or delaying them, and so He manifests them in accordance with what His wisdom requires and what His will has decreed. In this is evidence that He, glorified and exalted, knows things before they occur.
﴿And He knows what is in the land and the sea﴾ This is a conjunction of the report about the relation of His knowledge to observed things upon the report about the exclusivity of knowledge of unseen things to Him.
﴿And not a leaf falls but He knows it﴾ An exaggeration in the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of particulars.
﴿Nor a grain in the darknesses of the earth, nor anything moist or dry﴾ These are conjoined upon "leaf." His saying ﴿except that it is in a clear Record﴾ is a substitution from the first exception: a substitution of the whole, on the basis that the clear Record is the knowledge of Allah, glorified and exalted; or a substitution of inclusion, if by it is meant the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh). It has also been read in the nominative (marfu') by conjunction upon the position (mahall) of "leaf," or as nominative by way of the inceptive, with the predicate being "except that it is in a clear Record."

And it is He who takes you [in sleep] by night ("yunimukum fihi wa yurāqibukum", i.e., He makes you sleep during it and watches over you). The word *tawaffī* (taking in full, a term for taking a thing completely) is used metaphorically (*isti'āra*) for sleep, because sleep and death share the removal of awareness and discernment, for the root meaning of *tawaffī* is seizing a thing in its entirety. ﴿And He knows what you have earned by day﴾, i.e., what you have acquired (*kasabtum*) during it. He assigned sleep to the night and earning to the day in keeping with what is customary. ﴿Then He raises you up﴾, i.e., wakes you (*yūqiẓukum*). The word *ba'th* (raising) is used without restriction as a complement (*tarshīḥ*, a metaphor supported by a related term) to *tawaffī*. ﴿Therein﴾, i.e., in the day. ﴿That a term appointed may be fulfilled﴾, i.e., that the one who wakes may reach the last of the term appointed for him in this world. ﴿Then to Him is your return﴾, by death. ﴿Then He will inform you of what you used to do﴾, by requiting you for it.

It was also said that the verse is addressed to the disbelievers, and the meaning is that you are cast down like carcasses by night and earn sins by day, and that He, glorified and exalted, is aware of your deeds. He raises you from the graves concerning (p-166) that in which you have spent your lives, namely sleep by night and the earning of sins by day, so that He may fulfil the term He named and appointed for the resurrection of the dead and their recompense for their deeds. ﴿Then to Him is your return﴾ by reckoning. ﴿Then He will inform you of what you used to do﴾ by requital.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 61–62:

﴿And He is the Subduer over His servants, and He sends over you guardians (ḥafaẓah)﴾ angels who guard your deeds, and they are the noble recorders. The wisdom in this is that when the accountable person knows that his deeds are recorded against him and will be displayed before the heads of the witnesses, he is more restrained from sins. Also, when the servant trusts in the kindness of his master and relies on his pardon and concealment, he does not feel the same shame before Him that he would feel before his servants who are watching him. ﴿Until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him back﴾ the angel of death and his helpers. Ḥamzah recited "tawaffāhu" with an alif, with imālah (a vowel inclination toward i). ﴿And they do not fail﴾ through negligence or delay. It was also recited with the lighter form (takhfīf), and the meaning is: they do not exceed what has been prescribed for them, either by addition or by reduction.

﴿Then they are returned to God﴾ to His judgment and His recompense. ﴿their true Master (mawlāhum)﴾ who manages their affairs. ﴿the Truth (al-ḥaqq)﴾ the Just, who judges only with truth. It was also recited with the accusative (naṣb) as a form of praise. ﴿Surely to Him belongs the judgment﴾ on that day, no one else has any judgment in it. ﴿And He is the swiftest of reckoners﴾ He reckons all creatures in the time it takes to milk a sheep, and no reckoning preoccupies Him from another reckoning.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 63–64:

﴿Say, "Who rescues you from the darknesses of land and sea?"﴾ That is, from their hardships. The word "darkness" (ẓulumah) is used metaphorically for hardship, because the two share terror and the nullifying of sight; thus a severe day is called "a dark day" and "a day full of stars." Or it means from being swallowed up by the earth on land and drowned at sea.

Ya'qub recited yunjikum (with light stress, i.e., the form without doubling of the jim), and the meaning is one. ﴿You call upon Him humbly and secretly﴾, openly and privately, or with open and secret supplication. Abu Bakr recited khifyatan with a kasra here and in "al-A'raf," and it has also been read khiyfatan (fear). ﴿"If He rescues us from this, we will surely be among the thankful."﴾ This is on the assumption of an unstated verb of saying, i.e., "you say: 'If You rescue us...'" The Kufans recited anjana ("rescued us"), to agree with their saying tad'unahu (you call upon Him). "This" refers to the darkness.

﴿Say, "It is Allah who rescues you from it"﴾: the Kufans and Hisham read yunajjikum with doubling of the stress, while the rest read it lightly. ﴿And from every distress﴾, any grief other than these. ﴿Then you associate partners [with Him]﴾: you return to association and do not keep your covenant. The phrase "you associate partners" was used in place of "you do not give thanks," as an alert that whoever associates another in the worship of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is as though he had not worshipped Him at all.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 67–68:

﴿For every tidings﴾ — a news-report; he means by it either the punishment or the threat of it. ﴿There is a fixed time﴾ — a time of settlement and occurrence. ﴿And you will come to know﴾ — at its occurrence, in this world and in the Hereafter.

﴿And when you see those who engage in vain discourse concerning Our signs﴾ — by denying them, mocking them, and disparaging them. ﴿Then turn away from them﴾ — do not sit with them, and rise up from them. ﴿Until they engage in a discourse other than this﴾ — he returned the pronoun to the meaning of "signs," because they are the Qur'an. ﴿And if Satan should make you forget﴾ — by occupying you with his whisperings until you forget the prohibition. Ibn ʿAmir read ﴿yunassiyannaka﴾ with the doubled letter (tashdid). ﴿Then do not sit, after the remembrance﴾ — after you have remembered it. ﴿with the wrongdoing people﴾ — that is, with them. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun, to indicate that they wronged by placing denial and mockery in the place of affirmation and magnification.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 69:

﴿And upon those who are God-fearing (alladhina yattaqun) there is nothing﴾ — that is, nothing of the ugly deeds and words of those who sit with them is incumbent upon the God-fearing (al-muttaqin).

﴿of their reckoning﴾ — ﴿min hisabihim﴾: "min shay'" means some part of that for which they are called to account.

﴿but a reminder﴾ — ﴿wa lakin dhikra﴾: rather, it is incumbent upon them to remind them (yudhakkirunahum), a reminder (dhikra), and to prevent them from plunging into (al-khawd) and other ugly deeds, and to make their disapproval of them evident. The word may be in the accusative (nasb) as an infinitive (masdar), or in the nominative (raf') as in "wa lakin 'alayhim dhikra." It is not permissible to take it as a conjunction (ataf) upon the place (mahall) of "min shay'," because "min hisabihim" rejects it, nor upon "shay'" for that reason, and because "min" is not added (tuzad) in affirmative sentences.

﴿that perhaps they may be God-fearing﴾ — ﴿la'allahum yattaqun﴾: they abstain from that out of shame (haya') or out of dislike for causing them displeasure. It is also possible that the pronoun refers to those who are God-fearing, and the meaning is: perhaps they will remain steadfast in their piety and it will not be compromised by sitting with them.

It was narrated that the Muslims said: "If we were to stand up every time they mocked the Qur'an, we would not be able to sit in the Sacred Mosque and perform tawaf," so this verse was revealed.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 70:

﴿And leave those who have taken their religion as amusement and diversion﴾. That is, they built the matter of their religion upon whim and desire, and they practised a religion by which no benefit returns to them, neither in this world nor in the next, such as the worship of idols and the prohibition of the baheera and the saiba (kinds of animals). Or [it means] they took the religion laid upon them as amusement and diversion, in that they mocked it. Or they made their festival, which had been appointed as the time for their worship, a time of diversion and play. The meaning is: turn away from them and do not concern yourself with their deeds and their words. It is also permissible that this be a threat to them, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Leave Me with the one whom I created alone﴾. And whoever holds it to be abrogated by the verse of the sword takes it as a command to refrain from them and to leave off confronting them. ﴿And the life of this world has deceived them﴾, to the extent that they denied the resurrection.

﴿And remind by it﴾, that is, by the Qur'an, ﴿lest a soul be delivered over to ruin for what it has earned﴾: for fear that it be handed over to destruction and be held in pledge for its evil deeds. The root of ibsal (delivering over) and absl (prohibiting) is prevention, and from it comes "asad basil" (a brave lion), because its prey does not escape from it; and "al-basil" is the brave one, due to his refusal to yield to his opponent; and "hadha basil 'alayka" means "this is forbidden to you." ﴿It has no protector apart from God, nor any intercessor﴾ who would ward off the punishment from it. ﴿And if it offers every ransom﴾, and if it pays every ransom; and "al-'adl" means ransom, because it is equivalent to the one ransomed (al-mufda), and here it means the ransom, and "kull" is in the accusative as an infinitive (masdar). ﴿Nor will it be taken from it﴾: the verb is attributed to "minha" (from it) and not to its pronoun, unlike His saying: ﴿nor will any ransom be taken from it﴾, for that is the thing by which one is ransomed. ﴿Those are the ones who have been delivered over to ruin for what they earned﴾: that is, they were handed over to punishment because of their ugly deeds and their deviant beliefs. ﴿For them is a drink of scalding water and a painful punishment because they used to disbelieve﴾: this is an emphasis and an elaboration of that. The meaning is that they are between boiling water that churns in their bellies and fire that blazes upon their bodies because of their disbelief.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 71:

﴿Say: "Shall we call upon, instead of Allah, that which can neither benefit us nor harm us?"﴾ "Shall we worship" [instead of Allah] that which cannot benefit us or harm us, meaning, that which has no power to benefit or harm us. ﴿And be turned back on our heels?﴾ "And return to polytheism after Allah has guided us and rescued us from it and granted us Islam." ﴿Like one whom the devils have enticed﴾ like one whom the rebellious jinn have led away into the desert wastes. The verb is of the form istaf'ala (ist-if'al, the tenth form) from hawa, yahwi, hawyan, meaning "to go away." Hamzah recited "istahwahu" with a long alif and imalah (an inclining of the vowel). The place of the kaf (the particle "like") is in the accusative, as a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of "naruddu" (we are turned back), meaning: "resembling the one whom the devils have enticed"; or it is in the accusative as an adverbial of manner (masdar), meaning: "a turning back like the turning back of the one whom the devils have enticed." ﴿Bewildered in the earth﴾ perplexed, astray from the path. ﴿Who has companions﴾ for this one who has been enticed, a group of companions.

﴿Who call him to guidance﴾ calling him to the straight path, that they may show him the way; or "to the straight path." He called it guidance by naming the object with the verbal noun (masdar). ﴿Come to us﴾ they say to him: "Come to us." ﴿Say: Indeed, the guidance of Allah﴾ which is Islam ﴿is the [true] guidance﴾ alone, and whatever is other than it is misguidance. ﴿And we have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds﴾ this is part of what is said, coordinated (ʿatf) with "indeed the guidance of Allah." The lam is for giving the reason for the command, meaning: "we have been commanded with this in order that we submit." It has also been said that the lam here has the meaning of the bāʾ, and it has also been said that it is redundant (zāʾidah).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 72:

﴿And that you establish the prayer and fear Him.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) upon "that we may submit" (li-nuslima), i.e., "to submit to the Lord of the worlds and to establish the prayer." Or it is coordinated upon its position, as if it were said: "We have been commanded to submit and that you establish the prayer."

It is narrated that ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakr invited his father to the worship of idols, and so this was revealed.

On this basis, the Messenger ﷺ's command with this statement was a response concerning al-Ṣiddīq (raḍiya Allāh ʿanhu), in glorification of his station and in manifestation of the bond of unity that existed between them. ﴿And He it is to whom you will be gathered﴾ on the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 73:

﴿And He it is who created the heavens and the earth in truth.﴾ Standing by the truth and wisdom. ﴿And on the day He says, "Be," and it is, His word is the truth.﴾ This is a nominal sentence in which the predicate has been placed first, meaning: His word is the truth on the day He says it, just as you say, "Fighting is on Friday." The meaning is that He is the Creator of the heavens and the earths, and His word is the truth, effective in all existent things. It has also been said that "the day" (yawm) is in the accusative by coordination with "the heavens" (al-samawat), or with the pronoun in "fear Him" (wa-ttaquhu), or by an omitted verb indicated by "in truth." His word "is the truth" may be a subject and predicate, or the subject of "it is" (yakunu), in the sense of "and when He says to His word 'the truth', that is to His decree, 'Be,' and it is." What is meant is the time when He brings things into existence and originates them, or the time when the Resurrection occurs, so that the bringing into being is the gathering of the dead and their revival. ﴿And His is the dominion on the day the Trumpet is blown.﴾ Like His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿To whom belongs the dominion today? To God, the One, the Subduer.﴾ ﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed.﴾ That is, He is the Knower of the unseen. ﴿And He is the Wise, the Acquainted.﴾ Like a summary (fadhlaka) of the verse.

(p-169) ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar﴾ — this is an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to "his father." In the books of history, his name is said to be Tārikh, so it is said that both are his names, like Israel and Jacob. It is also said that the proper name is Tārikh and Āzar is a descriptive epithet, meaning "the old man" or "the crooked one." Perhaps the reason it is not declined (ghayr munṣarif) is that it is foreign (aʿjamī) and was treated as analogous to its pattern (muwāzin). Or it is a derived epithet from āzar (strength) or wizr (burden). The more likely view is that it is a foreign proper name on the pattern of fāʿil, like ʿĀbir and Shālikh. It is also said that it is the name of an idol he worshipped, and he was called by it because of his constant worship of it, or it was applied to him by deleting the genitive (ḥadhf al-muḍāf). It is also said that the intended meaning is the idol, and that it is in the accusative governed by a hidden verb explained by what follows, i.e., "Do you take Azar as a deity?" Then he said: ﴿Do you take idols as gods?﴾ as an explanation and confirmation. What supports this is that it was recited as "Āzaran" [with the hamza vowelled differently], "tattakhidhu aṣnāman," with the hamza of Āzar pronounced with a fatḥa or a kasra, and it is the name of an idol. Yaʿqūb recited it with a ḍamma, as a vocative (nidāʾ), and this indicates that it is a proper name. ﴿Indeed I see you and your people in manifest error﴾ — away from the truth. ﴿Manifest﴾ — clearly evident in its error.

﴿And thus did We show Abraham﴾ — and like this insight We granted him insight. This is a narration of a past state. It was also recited "tarā" with a *tāʾ* and the *malakūt* in the nominative, meaning that the signs of lordship made him see. ﴿the dominion (malakūt) of the heavens and the earth﴾ — their lordship and their sovereignty. It is also said: their wonders and marvels. Malakūt is the greatest form of dominion, and the *tāʾ* in it is for intensification (mubālagha). ﴿and that he might be among the certain (al-mūqinīn)﴾ — i.e., so that he might reason from evidence and so that he would be among them; or, We did that so that he would be among them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 76–77:

﴿So when the night covered him, he saw a star, and said: "This is my lord."﴾ This is a detailing and explanation of that. It is said that it is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) upon "Ibrahim said," and "Thus did We show" is a parenthetical interjection (iʿtiraḍ). His father and his people used to worship idols and stars, so he wanted to alert them to their misguidance and guide them to the truth through reflection and inference (istidlal). "The night covered him" means it concealed him with its darkness. The star was either Venus or Jupiter. His saying "This is my lord" was said as a manner of positing (waḍʿ), for the one who argues against a false view recounts it as the opponent says it and then refutes it. Or it was said by way of reflection and inference. He said it during his adolescence or at the beginning of the time of his maturity.

﴿Then, when it set﴾, that is, it disappeared. ﴿He said: "I do not love the things that set."﴾ Much less would he worship them, for moving and hiding behind veils indicates contingency (imkan) and origination in time (huduth), and contradicts divinity (uluhiyyah).

﴿Then, when he saw the moon rising﴾, beginning to ascend. ﴿He said: "This is my lord." Then, when it set, he said: "If my Lord does not guide me, I will surely be among the people who are astray."﴾ He acknowledged his own incapacity and sought help from his Lord in reaching the truth, for one cannot be guided to it except by His granting success. This was a guidance for his people and an alert to them, that the moon too, because its state changes, is not fit for divinity, and that whoever takes it as a god is astray.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 78–79:

﴿So when he saw the sun rising, he said: "This is my lord."﴾ The demonstrative noun (ism al-ishara, "this") is used to make the predicate masculine (li-tadhkir al-khabar), and to protect the Lord from the suspicion of femininity (wa-siyanatan li-l-Rabb 'an shubhat al-ta'nith).

﴿"This is greater."﴾ Its greatness is either for the sake of argument (istidlalan) or to display the opponent's doubt (izharan li-shubhat al-khasm). ﴿So when it set, he said: "O my people, I am free from what you associate [with Allah]."﴾ [He meant] the originated bodies (al-ajram al-muhdatha), which are in need of an originator (muhdith) who brings them into being and a specifier (mukhassis) who assigns them what they are particular to. Then, when he had disowned them, he turned toward their Originator and Creator (mujidiha wa-mubdi'ihi), to whom these contingent beings (al-mumkinat) point, and said:

﴿"Indeed, I have turned my face toward He who created the heavens and the earth, as a upright monotheist (hanifan), and I am not of the polytheists."﴾ He argued by the setting (al-uful) rather than the rising (al-buzugh), although the rising is also a change (intiqal), because the setting is more multiply indicative of [the contingent nature of what is changing] (li-ta'addud dalalatihi); and because he saw the star they worship at the middle of the sky when he attempted the inference (istidlal).

(p-170) ﴿And his people argued with him﴾, disputing with him about tawhid (the oneness of God). ﴿He said: Do you argue with me concerning God﴾, concerning His oneness, glorified and exalted is He. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, with a variant transmitted from Hisham, read ﴿أتُحاجُّونِّي﴾ with the lightening of the nun (takhfif al-nun, تَخْفِيفُ النُّونِ), meaning the doubled nun is pronounced as a single nun. ﴿And He has guided me﴾ to His oneness. ﴿And I do not fear what you associate with Him﴾, meaning I do not fear your deities at any time, because they cause no harm of their own and bring no benefit. ﴿Except that my Lord wills something﴾, meaning that He may afflict me with some harm from them. This is perhaps a reply to their warning him about their gods, and a threat to them of God's punishment. ﴿My Lord encompasses all things in knowledge﴾. It is as if this is the reason for the exception (istithna'), meaning that He has encompassed everything in His knowledge, so it is not far-fetched that it is within His knowledge that some harm from them should befall me. ﴿Will you not then remember﴾, so that you may distinguish between the sound and the corrupt, and between the capable and the incapable.

﴿And how should I fear what you have associated﴾, when no harm attaches to it? ﴿And you do not fear that you have associated with God﴾, when He is worthy of being feared with complete fear, because associating what is made with its Maker is a equating of the powerless, dependent creature with the capable entity that harms and benefits. ﴿For which He has sent down to you no authority﴾, meaning He has sent down no scripture for your association, or no proof has been established for it. ﴿So which of the two parties is more deserving of security﴾, meaning the monotheists or the polytheists? He did not say "which of us or you," in order to avoid praising himself. ﴿If you know﴾ what is truly deserving of being feared.
