Verse 82 of Surah al-An'am:

﴿Those who believe and do not mix their belief with wrongdoing (ẓulm), for them there is security, and they are the guided.﴾ This is a resumption (istinaf), either from him (God) or from God Himself, providing the answer to what was questioned. By "wrongdoing" (ẓulm) here is meant polytheism (shirk), according to what has been related: that when this verse was revealed it weighed heavily upon the Companions, and they said, "Which of us has not wronged himself?" Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "It is not what you think. It is rather what Luqman said to his son: ﴿O my son, do not associate anything with God; indeed, association is a tremendous wrongdoing.﴾" Belief in Him is not merely to affirm the existence of the Wise Creator (al-Sani' al-Hakim) while mixing this affirmation with associating others with Him. It has also been said that wrongdoing here means disobedience (ma'siyah).

﴿And that﴾ refers to the argument Abraham made against his people, from his words ﴿When the night covered him﴾ up to his words ﴿while they are guided﴾, or from his words ﴿Do you dispute with me﴾ up to it. ﴿Our argument, We gave it to Abraham﴾: We guided him to it, or We taught it to him. ﴿Against his people﴾ is connected to ﴿Our argument﴾ if ﴿that﴾ is taken as the predicate (*khabar*), and to an omitted element if it is taken as an apposition (*badal*). That is: We gave it to Abraham as an argument against his people.

﴿We raise by degrees whom We will﴾ in knowledge and wisdom. The Kufans and Ya'qub read ﴿دَرَجاتٍ﴾ with tanwin (nunation). ﴿Indeed your Lord is All-Wise﴾ in His elevating and abasing. ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of the state of the one He elevates and of his readiness for it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 84–85:

﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob; each We guided.﴾ That is, each of them. ﴿And Noah We guided before,﴾ before Abraham. He counted his guidance as a blessing upon Abraham, since he was his father, and the honour of a parent extends to the child. ﴿And of his offspring﴾: the pronoun refers to Abraham, peace be upon him, since the discussion is about him. It has also been said that it refers to Noah, peace be upon him, because he is nearer, and because Yunus (Jonah) and Lut (Lot) were not of the offspring of Abraham; for if it referred to Abraham, the explanation would be restricted to those mentioned in that verse and the one after it. Those mentioned in the third verse are a conjunction (ʿatf) upon Noah: ﴿David and Solomon and Job﴾. Job was the son of Amus, one of the descendants of ʿIs ibn Isaac. ﴿And Joseph and Moses and Aaron. Thus do We reward the good-doers﴾: that is, and We reward the good-doers with a reward like what We gave Abraham, by raising their ranks, multiplying their children, and placing prophethood among them.

﴿And Zachariah and John and Jesus﴾: he is the son of Mary, and mentioning him is evidence that "offspring" (dhurriyyah) includes the children of a daughter. ﴿And Elias﴾: it has been said he is Idris, the grandfather of Noah, in which case the explanation is restricted to those in the first verse. It has also been said he is one of the descendants of Aaron, brother of Moses. ﴿Each of the righteous﴾: those perfect in righteousness (ṣalāḥ), which is doing what is fitting and guarding against what is not fitting.

﴿And Isma'il, al-Yasa', Yunus and Lut﴾. Al-Yasa' is the son of Akhtub (Elisha). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read **اللَيْسَعَ** (*al-Layså'*) with a lam. **Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 6, verses 88–89:**

﴿That is the guidance of Allah﴾: a reference to what they adhered to. ﴿He guides whom He wills of His servants﴾: evidence that He bestows guidance upon them as an act of grace. ﴿And if they had associated [others with Him]﴾: that is, if these prophets, peace be upon them, had associated others with Allah despite their excellence and their elevated station. ﴿Their deeds would have been nullified, and all that they used to do would have been in vain﴾: they would have been like others in having their deeds nullified, with their reward lost.

﴿Those are the ones to whom We gave the Book﴾: he means by it the category (of Scripture). ﴿And the judgment﴾: wisdom, or the decisive settling of matters in accordance with what truth requires. ﴿And prophethood﴾: and messengership. ﴿If these [people] disbelieve in them﴾: that is, in these three things. ﴿These [people]﴾: meaning the Quraysh. ﴿Then We have entrusted them﴾: that is, to the upholding of them. ﴿To a people who are not disbelievers in them﴾: and they are the prophets, peace be upon them, who were mentioned, and those who follow them. It has also been said that they are the Ansar, or the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), or everyone who believed in him, or the Persians. It has also been said that they are the angels.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 90:

﴿Those are the ones whom God guided﴾. He means the prophets, upon them be prayers and peace, who were mentioned earlier. ﴿So follow their guidance﴾. He singled out their path for emulation. What is meant by "their guidance" is that upon which they all agreed: monotheism (tawhid) and the foundations of the religion (usul al-din), excluding the subsidiary matters (furu') in which they differed, for these are not a guidance attributed to all of them, and it is not possible to emulate all of them in them. Therefore there is no proof in this that he, upon him be peace, was bound by the law of those before him. The ha' in ﴿iqtadih﴾ is for pause (waqf). As for those who establish it in continuous recitation (darj) as a silent vowel, such as Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and 'Asim, they treat the connected reading as if it were a pause. Hamza and al-Kisa'i delete the ha' only in connected reading. Ibn 'Amir, according to the transmission of Ibn Dhakwan, prolongs it with a kasra, considering it a pronominal suffix of the verbal noun, and according to the transmission of Hisham, it is a kasra without prolongation.

﴿Say: I do not ask of you any reward for it﴾, i.e., for the conveying or for the Qur'an. ﴿A reward﴾, a wage from you, just as those prophets before me did not ask, and this is among the matters in which they were commanded to be emulated. ﴿It is not﴾, i.e., the conveying, or the Qur'an, or the purpose. ﴿But a reminder to the worlds﴾, i.e., nothing but an admonition and exhortation to them.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 91:**

﴿They did not measure God with His true measure﴾, meaning they did not know Him with His true knowledge in respect of His mercy and His bounties upon His servants. ﴿When they said: God did not send down anything upon any human being﴾, at the time they denied the revelation (*wahy*) and the sending of the messengers, peace be upon them. That is among the greatest of His mercy and the most majestic of His blessings. Or it refers to His wrath against the disbelievers and the severity of His seizing of them when they dared to utter this statement. The speakers were the Jews, who said this in exaggeration of their denial that the Qur'an was sent down, as shown by the refutation of their statement and the obligation placed on them by His words: ﴿Say: Who sent down the Book that Moses brought, a light and guidance for the people?﴾ The reading of the majority is ﴿تَجْعَلُونَهُ قَرَاطِيسَ تُبْدُونَهَا وَتُخْفُونَ كَثِيرًا﴾ (*tajʿalūnahu qarāṭīsa tubdūnahā wa tukhfūna kathīran*, "you make it into scrolls, you display some of it and conceal much"), with *tāʾ* (the second person, "you"). Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read it with *yāʾ* (the third person, "they") (*bi-l-yāʾ*), taking it as continuing the sense of ﴿قالوا﴾ (*qālū*, "they said") and ﴿وما قدروا﴾ (*wa-mā qadarū*, "they did not measure"). This implies a rebuke of them for their poor ignorance of the Torah (*al-Tawrah*, the Torah) and a censure of them for dividing it: they displayed a part that they selected and wrote on scattered sheets, and concealed a part that they did not desire.

It is narrated that Malik ibn al-Sayf said this when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) angered him by saying: "I adjure you by God, who sent down the Torah to Moses, do you find in it that God hates the fat rabbi (*al-ḥibr al-samīn*)?" He said: "Yes, God hates the fat rabbi." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ), peace be upon him, said: "You are the fat rabbi."

It is said that the speakers were the polytheists, and the argument against them was based on the sending down of the Torah, because it was among the well-known and widespread matters among them. For this reason they used to say: "If the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than they." And you were taught through the tongue of Muhammad (ﷺ) ﴿what you did not know, neither you nor your fathers﴾, in addition to what is in the Torah and as a clarification of what was obscure to you and to your fathers, who were more knowledgeable than you. A parallel to this is His words: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an relates to the Children of Israel most of what they differ over﴾. It is also said that the address is to those among the Quraysh who had believed. ﴿Say: God﴾, meaning God sent it down, or God sent it down. He commanded him to answer on their behalf, to indicate that the answer is fixed and that no other answer is possible, and to alert them to the fact that they were so confounded that they could not answer. ﴿Then leave them in their discourse﴾, meaning in their falsehoods, so there is no blame on you after conveying the message and establishing the proof. ﴿Playing﴾ is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring to the first "they" (*hum*). The adverbial phrase (*al-ẓarf*) is connected to *dhar-hum* (leave them), or to *yalʿabūna* (playing), or is a circumstantial clause referring to its object, or the subject of *yalʿabūna*, or to the second "they" (*hum*), with the adverbial phrase connected to the first.

This is a book We have sent down, blessed: abundant in benefit and good. ﴿Confirming what is before it﴾, meaning the Torah, or the books that came before it. ﴿And that you may warn the Mother of Towns﴾ is coordinated with what the word "blessed" implies, i.e. "for blessings, and that you may warn"; or it is a causal clause for an omitted element, i.e. "and that you may warn the people of the Mother of Towns, We have sent it down." Mecca was named thus because it is the qibla (direction of prayer), the pilgrimage site and gathering place of the people of the towns, and the greatest of the towns in standing.

It is also said: it is because the earth was spread out (dukhiya) from beneath it, or because it is the place of the first House set up for mankind. Abu Bakr, on the authority of ʿAsim, read "yundhira" with a ya' (i.e. "that it may warn"), the subject being the Book. ﴿And those around it﴾ means the people of the East and the West. ﴿Those who believe in the Hereafter believe in it, and they guard their prayers﴾: for whoever believes in the Hereafter fears the consequence, and fear does not cease to drive him to reflection and contemplation until he believes in the Prophet and the Book. The pronoun may refer to either of them. He also keeps to obedience; the specification of prayer is because it is the pillar of the religion and the sign of faith.

(p-173) ﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents a lie against God﴾, by claiming that He has sent him as a prophet, like Musaylimah and al-Aswad al-Ansi; or by fabricating rulings in His name, like Amr ibn Luhayy and his followers. ﴿Or says, "It has been revealed to me," when nothing has been revealed to him﴾, like Abdullah ibn Sa'd ibn Abi Sarh. [He used to write for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). When the verse ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾ was revealed, and he reached His words, ﴿then We produced him as another creation﴾, Abdullah said, ﴿So blessed is God, the best of creators﴾, marvelling at the detailed creation of man. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Write it down, for it was revealed thus." Abdullah then doubted and said: "If Muhammad is truthful, then it has been revealed to me just as it was revealed to him; and if he is lying, then I have said just as he said."]

﴿And who says, "I will reveal the like of what God has revealed"﴾, like those who said, "If we wished, we would say the like of this." ﴿And if only you could see when the wrongdoers﴾: the object has been omitted because the adverbial phrase indicates it, meaning, "And if only you could see the wrongdoers." ﴿in the agonies of death﴾: its hardships, from ghamara, meaning water overwhelming someone when it covers him. ﴿while the angels extend their hands﴾: they seize their souls like an insistent, harsh creditor, or with punishment. ﴿"Bring out your souls"﴾: that is, they say to them, "Bring them out to us from your bodies," as harshness and rebuke towards them; or, "Bring them out from the punishment and free them from our hands." ﴿"Today"﴾: they mean the time of death, or the extended period from death to an endless end.

﴿"You will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation"﴾: that is, of humiliation; they mean the punishment that includes severity and disgrace. Its attribution to humiliation is due to its firmness and its being established in it. ﴿"for what you used to say about God other than the truth"﴾, such as claiming a son and a partner for Him, and claiming prophethood and revelation falsely. ﴿"and you used to be arrogant towards His signs"﴾, so you did not reflect upon them, nor did you believe.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on Surah 6, verse 94:

﴿And you have certainly come to Us﴾ for reckoning and recompense. ﴿Alone (furādā)﴾: separated from wealth, children, and all else of the worldly things you preferred, or separated from the helpers and idols that you claimed would be your intercessors. It is the plural of *fard* (single), and the *alif* is for the feminine, as in *kusālā* (the plural of *kaslān*, "lazy"). It has also been read as *firādā*, like *rikhāl* (plural of *rakhl*, "young female sheep"); as *farādin*, like *thalāth* (plural of *thalātha*, "three"); and as *fardā*, like *saknā* (the feminine form of *sakrān*, "drunk"). ﴿Just as We created you the first time﴾ is a *badal* (substitution, or apposition) for *furādā*, meaning in the state in which you were born, alone. Or it is a second *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative), if multiple *ḥāl*s are permitted. Or it is a *ḥāl* from the pronoun in *furādā*, meaning resembling the beginning of your creation: naked, barefoot, uncircumcised, and without distinguishing marks. Or it is an attribute of the verbal noun in *ji'tumūnā*, meaning "Our coming (to Us) just as We created you." ﴿And you have left behind what We bestowed upon you﴾: what We granted you in the world, so that you became preoccupied with it and neglected the Hereafter. ﴿Behind your backs﴾: you sent forward nothing of it, and you did not carry away even a speck (*naqīr*).

﴿And We do not see with you your intercessors whom you claimed were partners in you﴾: that is, partners of God in His lordship over you and in the right to be worshipped by you.

﴿Your ties have indeed been severed among you﴾: your connection was cut and your unity scattered. *Al-bayn* is one of the words with opposite meanings (*al-aḍdād*), used both for connection and for separation. It was also said that it is the adverbial noun (*al-ẓarf*) to which the verb has been attributed by extension (*ittisā'an*), and the meaning is: the severance has occurred between you. This is supported by the reading of Nāfi', al-Kisā'ī, and Ḥafs on the authority of 'Āṣim, in the accusative (*bayna-kum* with *naṣb*), by implying the subject, since the preceding words indicate it. Or it has been made to stand in place of its qualified noun, and the original is "the severance has occurred between what is between you," and this has also been read. ﴿And what you used to claim has vanished from you﴾: it was lost and perished. ﴿What you used to claim﴾: that they were your intercessors, or that there would be no resurrection and no recompense.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 95:

﴿Indeed, Allah is the cleaver of the grain and the date-pit﴾, [meaning He causes] the sprouting of plants and trees. It has also been said that what is meant is the split that is in the wheat-grain and the date-pit. ﴿He brings forth the living from the dead﴾, by which he means what grows of animals and plants, in order to match what came before it. ﴿From the dead﴾, meaning that which does not grow, such as sperm-drops and seeds.

﴿And the Bringer-forth of the dead from the living﴾: and the Bringer-forth of that from animals and plants. He mentioned it with the form of the noun (ism) by analogy with "the cleaver of the grain," since his saying "He brings forth the living" stands in the position of an explanation (bayan) of it. ﴿That is Allah﴾, that is, that Giver of life and Causer of death is the One who alone deserves worship.

﴿Then how are you turned away?﴾ You are diverted from Him toward other than Him.

﴿Fāliq al-iṣbāḥ﴾ (the Splitter of the dawn): one who splits the column of morning (ʿamūd al-ṣubḥ) from the darkness of night, or from the whiteness of day. Or it means one who splits the darkness of dawn (ẓulmat al-iṣbāḥ), which is the dimness (al-ghabsh) that follows it. Al-iṣbāḥ in origin is the verbal noun (maṣdar) of aṣbaḥa, meaning he entered the morning (al-ṣabāḥ), and it was then used as a name for the dawn (al-ṣubḥ). It was also recited with an open hamza, as aflāq (plural), and it was recited as fāliqun al-iṣbāḥa in the accusative (naṣb) for praise (al-madḥ).

﴿Wa-jaʿala al-layla sakanan﴾ (and He made the night a place of rest): a place in which the weary find rest from the day, because of their repose in it, from sakana ilayhi, meaning he found tranquillity and comfort in it. Or it means that creatures dwell in it, from the words of Exalted God: ﴿That you may rest therein﴾. Its accusative (naṣb) is governed by a verb indicated by jāʿil, not by jāʿil itself, since jāʿil has the sense of the past tense. This is supported by the recitation of the Kufans (al-Kūfiyyūn), wa-jaʿala al-layla, taking it as coordinated with the preceding word in meaning, since fāliq has the sense of faraqa (he split), and for this reason it was recited so. Or it is governed by jāʿil, meaning that the night was made continuous through the different times. On this view, ﴿wa-al-shamsa wa-al-qamar﴾ (and the sun and the moon) may be coordinated with the position (maḥall) of al-layl, and the recitation of both in the genitive (jarr) supports this. The better reading is their accusative, governed by a supposed jaʿala. It was also recited in the nominative (raf), as a subject (mubtadaʾ), with the predicate omitted, meaning majʿūlānī (both are made).

﴿Ḥusbānan﴾ (as a reckoning): that is, according to different orbits by which times are reckoned, and by which they form the science of reckoning (ʿilm al-ḥusbān). It is the verbal noun of ḥasaba (with a fatḥa), just as al-ḥisbān (with a kasra) is the verbal noun of ḥasiba. It was also said that it is the plural of ḥisāb, like shihāb and shuhbān.

﴿Dhālika﴾ (that): a reference to their being made a reckoning, meaning that this motion by precise calculation.

﴿Taqdīr al-ʿazīz﴾ (is the decree of the Almighty): He who subdued them and set them in motion in the specific manner.

﴿Al-ʿalīm﴾ (the All-Knowing): with regard to their governance and the most beneficial of the possible courses (tadāwīr) for them.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 97–98:**

﴿It is He who placed for you the stars﴾: He created them for you. ﴿So that you may be guided by them in the darknesses of land and sea﴾: in the darknesses of the night, on land and at sea. Their attribution to land and sea is for association (*mulabasah*), or it means in the confusing paths. He called them "darknesses" by way of metaphor (*isti'arah*, the use of a word in a figurative sense). This singles out some of their benefits for mention after summarizing them with His words "for you." ﴿We have detailed the signs﴾: We explained them one by one. ﴿For a people who know﴾: for they are the ones who benefit from them.

﴿It is He who produced you from a single soul﴾: this is Adam, peace be upon him. ﴿So there is a place of lodging and a place of storage﴾: that is, for you there is lodging in the loins, or above the earth, and storage in the wombs, or beneath the earth, or it is a place of lodging and storage. Ibn Kathir and the two Basran readers read it with a kasra on the qaf, as an active participle (*ism fa'il*, the noun of the doer), so "mustaqirr" means the one who settles. "Mustawda'" is then a passive participle (*ism maf'ul*, the noun of the one acted upon), meaning: among you is one who settles and among you is one who is stored, because settling is among us and storage is not. ﴿We have detailed the signs for a people who understand﴾: "those who know" is mentioned with the stars because their matter is manifest, and "those who understand" is mentioned with the creation of the children of Adam because their production from a single soul and their turning between varying states is subtle and obscure, requiring the use of insight and careful scrutiny.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 99:

﴿And it is He who sends down water from the sky﴾: from the clouds, or from the direction of the sky. ﴿Then We bring forth﴾: this is a shift in address (talwin al-khitab).

﴿By it﴾: by the water, ﴿the growth of every thing﴾: every kind of plant grew. The meaning is the manifestation of power in producing diverse, varied kinds from one water, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Watered with one water, yet We make some of them excel others in produce﴾ (p-175). ﴿Then We bring forth from it﴾: from the plants or from the water. ﴿Green﴾: something green, it is said akhdar (green) like a'war (one-eyed) and 'awar, and it is what emerges from the grain, branching out. ﴿We bring forth from it﴾: from the green. ﴿Grain piled up﴾: this is the spike of grain. ﴿And from the palm trees, from their spathes, clusters hanging low﴾: that is, We bring forth from the palm trees a palm [growth] whose spathes are clusters; or from the palm trees there is something from its spathes that are clusters. It is permissible that "min al-nakhl" is the predicate of qinwan, and "min tal'iha" is a substitute for it. The meaning: and resulting from the spathes of the palm are clusters, which are the bunches, the plural of qinw, like sinwan, the plural of sinw. It was also read with a damma on the qaf, like dhi'b and dhu'ban, and with a fatha, as a collective noun, since fi'lan is not among the patterns of plurals. ﴿Hanging low﴾: near to the reach, or close-set, some of them near to others. The reason it mentions only these and not their opposite is that they indicate it and for the increase of blessing in them. ﴿And gardens of grapes﴾: conjoined to "the growth of every thing." Nafi' read it in the nominative, as a new subject: that is, "and for you" or "then there are gardens," or "from the vine are gardens." It is not permissible to conjoin it to "qinwan," since grapes do not grow from the palm tree. ﴿And the olive and the pomegranate﴾: also conjoined to "growth," or put in the accusative for specification, due to the esteem of these two kinds among them. ﴿Similar and dissimilar﴾: a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pomegranate, or from all of them; that is, some of that is similar and some is dissimilar in form, measure, color and taste. ﴿Look at its fruit﴾: that is, the fruit of each one of those. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma on the tha' and the mim, which is the plural of thamara, like khashaba and khashab, or thimar, like kitab and kutub. ﴿When it bears fruit﴾: when it brings out its fruit, how it bears fruit, meager, from which hardly any benefit is derived.

﴿And its ripening﴾: and to the state of its ripeness, or to a ripened one, how it returns large, beneficial and delicious. It is originally a verbal noun of "yani'at al-thamar" when it ripened. It is said to be the plural of yani', like tajir and tajr. It was also read with a damma, which is a dialectal variant of it, and yani'uh. ﴿Indeed in that are signs for a people who believe﴾: that is, signs indicating the existence of the Capable, the Wise, and His oneness, for the origination of diverse kinds and varied species from one origin, and their transfer from state to state, cannot occur except by the origination of a capable One who knows their details, and who prefers what His wisdom requires among what is possible for their states, and whom no rival opposing Him or adversary contending with Him can prevent from His act. For this reason, He follows it with a rebuke of those who associate others with Him and a refutation of them, saying:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 100:

﴿And they made the jinn partners with God﴾, i.e., the angels, by worshipping them, and they said: "The angels are the daughters of God." He called them jinn because they are hidden (ijtinan), to belittle their status; or [it refers to] the devils, because they obeyed them as God, exalted is He, is obeyed; or they worshipped idols through their (the devils') embellishment and incitement; or they said: God is the creator of good and of everything beneficial, and Satan is the creator of evil and of everything harmful, as is the opinion of the Dualists (al-thanawiyya).

The second object of "they made ... partners with God" is shurakaa'; "al-jinn" is a substitute (badal) for shurakaa', or [the phrase reads] shurakaa' al-jinn, and "li-Llah" is attached to shurakaa', or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from it. It has been recited as "al-Jinnu" with a nominative vowel, as if it were said: "Who are they?" and it was answered: "al-Jinn." And "al-Jinni" with a genitive vowel, in an annexation (idafa) for clarification (li-l-tabyin).

﴿And He created them﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) with "qad" implied, and the meaning is: while they knew that God is their creator, not the jinn, and he who creates is not like he who does not create. It has been recited as "wa-khalaqahum" (and they created them), coordinated (ataf) upon "al-jinn," meaning: and [they made partners] what they fashion of idols; or upon "shurakaa'," meaning: and they attributed to Him their fabrication (ikhtilafahum) of falsehood, when they ascribed it to Him.

﴿And they invented for Him﴾ means they fabricated and forged for Him. Nafi' read it with a doubled ra' (wa-kharrquu, "khariqu"), for intensification (lil-takthir). It has been recited as "wa-harrafu," meaning: they fabricated/falsified.

﴿sons and daughters﴾: the Jews said "Uzayr is the son of God," the Christians said "the Messiah is the son of God," and the Arabs said "the angels are the daughters of God."

﴿without knowledge﴾ means without them knowing the reality of what they said, and without them having any evidence for it. It is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the waw [of "wa-kharaqu"], or [it is] an infinitive (masdar), meaning: fabrication without knowledge.

﴿Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they describe﴾, which is that He has a partner or a son.

﴿The Originator of the heavens and the earth﴾. This is an idafa (construct phrase) of the sifa mushabbaha (the attributive adjective, a form resembling the active participle, meaning a quality that is constant in its bearer) to its agent, or to the adverbial phrase (zarf), as in their saying: "Treachery is established," meaning that He has no equal in them, the two. It is said that its meaning is "the Originator" (al-mubdi'), and the discussion of this has already passed. Its being in the nominative is either as a predicate of an omitted subject, or as a subject whose predicate is what follows.

﴿How can He have a child?﴾ That is: from where, or how, can He have a child?

﴿And He has no consort﴾ from whom a child would come. It is also read with the letter ya' (yakun), either because of the separation (between the verb and its feminine subject) or because the noun refers to God, or to the damir al-sha'n (the pronoun of the matter).

﴿And He created all things, and He is Knower of all things﴾, nothing hidden from Him is concealed. He did not say "bihi" (with it) because that would open the possibility of specifying the first (the creation), and the verse contains evidence for the negation of a child from several aspects:

(The first: the heavens and the earths are among His originated creations, and although they are of the kind described as begetting, they are free of it because of their permanence and the long duration of their existence. So He is more worthy of being exalted above it. Or: the offspring of a thing is like it, and He has no like, so there is no child.)

(The second: what is understood by a child is that which is born of a male and a female of the same kind, and God, glorified and exalted, is far above being of the same kind.)

(The third: the child is equal to the parent (kufu'), and He has no equal, for two reasons. The first: everything other than Him is His creation, so it cannot be equal to Him. The second: He, glorified and exalted, is knowing of all the known things by His essence, and others are not so, by consensus (ijma', the agreement of the scholars).)

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 6, verses 102–103:**

﴿Such is﴾ is a demonstrative referring to the one described by the attributes mentioned before it, and it is the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of the sentence). ﴿Allah is your Lord; there is no god but He, the Creator of all things﴾ are successive predicates (akhbar mutaradifah). It is also permissible for some of them to be a substitute (badal, apposition) or an attribute (sifah, adjective), and some of them to be the predicate (khabar). ﴿So worship Him﴾ is a ruling (hukm) caused by (musabbab 'an) the content of these statements, for whoever combines these attributes deserves to be worshipped. ﴿And He is Guardian over all things﴾ means: He, together with those attributes, is the one who manages your affairs, so entrust them to Him, and seek through His worship the fulfilment of your aims. And He is Watcher over your deeds, so He will recompense you for them.

﴿Vision does not encompass Him﴾ means: the sights do not encompass Him. ﴿Abṣār﴾ is the plural of baṣar, which is the faculty of sight, though it may be applied to the eye insofar as it is its locus. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 104–105:

﴿Indeed there have come to you clear evidences (baṣā'ir) from your Lord.﴾ Baṣā'ir is the plural of baṣīrah, and for the soul it is like sight (baṣar) for the body. The proof (dalālah) was named by it because it makes the truth manifest to the soul and causes it to see (tubaṣṣiruhā) by means of it. ﴿So whoever sees﴾ means whoever sees the truth and believes in it. ﴿then it is for his own self﴾ that he sees, because his soul benefits from it. ﴿And whoever is blind﴾ to the truth and goes astray. ﴿then against it﴾ is its burden (wabāluh). ﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾; I am only a warner, and Allah, glorified and exalted, is the Guardian over you, who preserves your deeds and recompenses you for them. This is a statement that was uttered on the tongue of the Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿And thus do We vary the verses﴾. Like that variation (taṣrīf) We vary, and it is the carrying out of the meaning that revolves among successive meanings, from ṣarf, which is the transfer of a thing from one state to another. ﴿And that they may say, "You have studied (darasta)"﴾, that is, and that they may say, "You have studied (darasta) Our variation." The lām is the lām of consequence (lām al-'āqibah). Dars means recitation and teaching. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read dāraslat, meaning they studied with the People of the Book and discussed with them. Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read darasat, from the verb "to become effaced" (durūs), meaning these verses became old and faded, like their saying, "the fables of the ancients." It was also read "darusat" with a damma on the ra', as an intensification of durisat, and "durisat" in the passive form, meaning "they were recited" or "they were effaced." Dāraslat may also mean "darasat" (she studied), or the Jews studied with Muhammad (ﷺ), and their pronoun was omitted without mention because of their being well known for study. Darasna means they were effaced, and darasa means Muhammad (ﷺ) studied. Dirasat means "ancient" or "possessing study," like His saying, ﴿in a pleasing life﴾. ﴿And that We may make it clear﴾: the lām is in its original sense, because making clear is the intended purpose of the variation. The pronoun refers to the verses in terms of their meaning, or to the Qur'an even though it is not mentioned because it is known, or to the verbal noun. ﴿For a people who know﴾, for they are the ones who benefit from it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 106–107:

﴿Follow what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾, by adopting it as your religion (al-tadayyun bihi). ﴿There is no deity except Him﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tirad), by which the obligation of following is emphasized; or it is an emphatic circumstantial clause (hal mu'akkidah) from "your Lord," meaning [He is] singular in divinity. ﴿And turn away from the polytheists﴾, and do not concern yourself with their statements or pay heed to their opinions. As for one who holds that this verse was abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword, he understands "turning away" as encompassing refraining from harming them (al-kaff 'anhum).

This is evidence that He, glory be to Him and exalted, does not will the faith of the disbelievers, and that His will is necessarily realized. ﴿And We have not appointed you over them as a guardian﴾, a watcher (raqiban). ﴿Nor are you a manager over them﴾, one who takes charge of their affairs.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 108:

﴿And do not revile those whom they invoke besides Allah﴾, i.e., do not mention their deities that they worship with the ugly qualities that are in them.

﴿Lest they revile Allah in enmity﴾, transgressing beyond the truth into falsehood. ﴿Without knowledge﴾, out of ignorance of Allah, glorified and exalted is He, and of what must be mentioned about Him. Ya'qub (Ya'qub ibn Ishaq al-Hadrami) read ʿadwan (عَدْوًا). It is said: ʿadā fulānun ʿadwan, and ʿudūwan, and ʿadāʾan, and ʿudwānan (all meaning he transgressed).

It is narrated: "He, upon him be blessings and peace, used to criticize their deities, so they said: 'Either you stop reviling our deities, or we will satirize your God.' So this verse was revealed."

It is also said that the Muslims used to revile them, so they were forbidden, lest their reviling become a cause for them to revile Allah, glorified and exalted is He. In this is evidence that when obedience leads to a greater disobedience, it becomes obligatory to abandon it, for that which leads to evil is itself evil. ﴿Thus We have made attractive to every community their deeds﴾, of good and evil, by creating what enables them to do them and inclines them toward them, through granting success (tawfiq) and abandonment (takhdhil). It is permissible to restrict "deeds" to evil and "every community" to the disbelievers, because the discussion concerns them, and the thing being compared to is the making attractive to them of reviling Allah. ﴿Then to their Lord is their return, and He will inform them of what they used to do﴾, by calling them to account and recompensing them for it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 109–110:

﴿And they swore by Allah their most emphatic oaths﴾: (jahda aymanihim) is a verbal noun (masdar) in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (hal). What prompted them to this oath and its emphasis was their insistence upon the Messenger (ﷺ) in demanding signs and their belittling of what they had already seen of them. ﴿If a sign came to them﴾ from among their proposed suggestions, ﴿they would surely believe in it. Say: "The signs are only with Allah"﴾: He is capable of them, manifesting from them whatever He wills, and none of them is within my power and will. ﴿And what would make you aware﴾: (wa ma yush'irukum), meaning, "what would inform you," is a rhetorical interrogative of denial. ﴿That they﴾: i.e., that the proposed sign, ﴿when it comes, they will not believe﴾: i.e., you do not know that they will not believe. He denied the cause as an exaggeration in negating the effect, and in this there is an admonition that He, glorified and exalted, only did not send them because He knows that when they come, they will not believe in them. It has also been said that "la" is extra (lā mazīda). It has also been said that "anna" carries the meaning of "la'alla" (perhaps), and it was read as la'allaha. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim, and Ya'qub read innaha with a kasra, as if he said: "And what would make you aware of what will come from them?" Then He informed you of what He knew of them. The address is to the believers, for they wished for the coming of the sign out of hope for their faith, so it was revealed. It has also been said that the address is to the polytheists, when Ibn 'Amir and Hamzah read "la tu'minun" with a ta'.

(p-178) It was also read: "wa ma yush'iruhum annaha idha ja'athum," in which case it is a denial directed at them regarding their oath, meaning: "And what would make them aware that their hearts at that time were not sealed as they were at the revelation of the Qur'an and other signs, so that they would believe in them?"

﴿And We turn about their hearts and their sight﴾: it is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon "they will not believe," meaning: "And what would make you aware that We, at that time, turn their hearts away from the truth so that they do not comprehend it, and their sight so that they do not perceive it, and so they do not believe in them. ﴿Just as they did not believe in it﴾: i.e., in what was sent down of the signs. ﴿The first time﴾ ﴿And We leave them in their transgression, wandering blindly﴾: We leave them bewildered, not guiding them with the guidance of the believers. It was also read: "wa yuqallibu" and "wa yadharuhum" in the third person, and "tuqallabu" in the passive voice with the attribution to the hearts.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 111:

﴿And even if We had sent down to them the angels, and the dead had spoken to them, and We had gathered together against them all things face to face﴾ as they proposed, saying: "Why were the angels not sent down upon us? Or let us see our Lord?" Or "Bring us a sign," or "You come with Allah and the angels as a group" (qabilan). Qabilan and qubulan are the plural of qabil, in the sense of kafil (guarantor), meaning: guarantors of what they gave good news of and warned of. Or qabil is the plural of qabilah, in the sense of groups. Or it is a verbal noun in the sense of "confrontation," like qubulan, and this is the reading of Nafi' and Ibn Amir. In all these senses it is a circumstantial accusative (hal) of kull (all), and this is permissible because of its generality.

﴿They would not believe﴾ because the judgment of disbelief had already been passed upon them. ﴿Unless Allah wills﴾ is an exception from the most general of circumstances, meaning: they will not believe in any circumstance except the circumstance of Allah the Exalted's will for their faith. It has also been said that the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), and this is a clear proof against the Mu'tazilah. ﴿But most of them are ignorant﴾ that, even if they were given every sign, they would not believe; so they swear by Allah with their most solemn oaths concerning what they do not perceive. For this reason, ignorance is attributed to most of them, although absolute ignorance encompasses all of them. Or it means: "But most Muslims are ignorant that they will not believe, so they wish for the sign to be sent down, hoping for their faith."

**Translation:**

﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy﴾. That is, just as We appointed an enemy for you, We appointed for every prophet who came before you an enemy. This is evidence that the enmity of the disbelievers toward the prophets, peace be upon them, comes by the act and creation of God, glorified and exalted be He. ﴿Devils of mankind and jinn﴾: the rebellious ones of both groups. This phrase is a substitution (*badal*) for "enemy," or the first object of "We appointed," with "enemy" as its second object. The phrase *li-kulli* ("for every") is either connected to it, or it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) derived from it.

﴿They inspire one another﴾: the devils of the jinn whisper to the devils of mankind, or some of the jinn to others, and some of mankind to others. ﴿Varnished speech﴾: the falsehoods that are embellished, from *zakhrafahu*, meaning he adorned it, when he decorated it. ﴿Delusion﴾ is either an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*), or a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause.

﴿And if your Lord had willed﴾ their faith, ﴿they would not have done it﴾. That is, they did not do that, meaning hostility toward the prophets, peace be upon them, and the inspiring of embellished speech. The pronoun may also refer to the inspiring, the embellishment, or the delusion. This too is evidence against the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school that holds human beings create their own acts). ﴿So leave them and what they fabricate﴾: and their disbelief.

﴿And that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline to it﴾: this is conjoined to "delusion" if that is taken as the cause, or it is connected to an omitted element, meaning: and so that this may happen, We appointed for every prophet an enemy. The Mu'tazilah, when they were pressed by this verse, said: the *lam* here is *lam al-'aqibah* (the "lam of consequence," indicating a result not intended by the act), or it is the *lam* of oath, its vowel being *kasra* because the verb was not emphasized with the *nun*, or it is the *lam* of command. Its weakness is most evident. *Al-sagh'* means inclination. The pronoun refers to what the pronoun in *fa'aluhu* refers to. ﴿And that they may be pleased with it﴾ for themselves. ﴿And that they may commit﴾ and acquire, ﴿what they are committing﴾ of sins.

(p-179) ﴿Should I seek a judge other than God?﴾ This is on the presumption of a spoken statement, meaning: Say to them, O Muhammad, "Should I seek other than God as a judge who will decide between me and you and distinguish the one of us who is in the right from the one who is in the wrong?" "Other than" (ghayr) is the object of abtaghi (seek), and "a judge" (hakaman) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from it, though it is possible that it is the reverse. Hakaman is more intensive than hakim (judge), and for this reason it is not applied as a description to anyone other than the just. ﴿And He it is who has sent down to you the Book﴾, meaning the Qur'an, the inimitable (al-mu'jiz).

﴿Explained in detail﴾, meaning clarifying within it the truth and falsehood in such a way that it negates confusion and ambiguity. In this there is an indication that the Qur'an, by its inimitability and its affirmation, suffices as a substitute for all other signs. ﴿And those to whom We have given the Book know that it has been sent down from your Lord in truth﴾. This is a confirmation of the indication of inimitability that the Qur'an is a truth sent down from God, glorified and exalted be He. The People of the Book know this through its confirmation of what they have. Although the Prophet, peace be upon him, had not studied their books nor associated with their scholars, all of them are described as having knowledge because most of them know, and whoever does not know is able to acquire it with minimal reflection. It has also been said that the intended meaning is the believers among the People of the Book. Ibn 'Amir and Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read munazzal with the doubled letter (tashdid). ﴿So do not be among the doubters﴾ concerning whether they know this, or concerning whether it is sent down, given the denial and disbelief of most of them towards it; so this falls under the category of stirring up (tahyij), like His saying, exalted be He: "And do not be among the polytheists." Or the address of the Messenger, peace be upon him, is an address to the community. It has also been said that the address is to everyone, in the sense that since the proofs have converged on its authenticity, no one should doubt it.

And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled [in truth and justice]: it has reached its ultimate end, (namely) His reports, His rulings, and His promises. [Truthful (ṣidqan)]: in the reports and the promises.

[And just (ʿadlan)]: in the judgments and the rulings. The accusative of both (ṣidqan and ʿadlan) may be read as a specifier (tamyīz), as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), or as an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu).

[None can alter His words]: no one can change any part of them into something more truthful and more just. Or: no one is able to distort them openly and publicly, as was done with the Torah, on the understanding that what is meant by "words" is the Qur'an; in that case it is a guarantee from God, glorified and exalted be He, of its preservation, like His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is We who have sent down the Reminder, and indeed We will be its guardian﴾. Or: there is no prophet and no scripture after it that would abrogate it (naskh) and change its rulings.

The Kufans and Yaʿqub read "kalimatu rabbika" (in the singular), meaning what He has spoken, or the Qur'an.

[And He is the All-Hearing] of what they say, [the All-Knowing] of what they conceal, so He will not leave them unpunished.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 116:

﴿And if you obey most of those on earth﴾ i.e., most of the people, meaning the disbelievers, or the ignorant, or the followers of desires (ahl al-hawa). It is also said that "the earth" refers to the land of Makkah. ﴿they will mislead you from the way of Allah﴾ from the path that leads to Him, for the one who has gone astray, in most cases, only commands what contains misguidance. ﴿They follow nothing but assumption﴾ and this is their assumption that their forefathers were upon the truth, or their ignorances and corrupt opinions, for ẓann (assumption) is applied to what is the opposite of ʿilm (knowledge). ﴿And they are only guessing﴾ they lie against Allah, glory be to Him, in what they attribute to Him, such as taking a son for Him, making the worship of idols a means of reaching Him, declaring carrion lawful, and forbidding the baḥāʾir (slit-eared she-camels). Or they suppose that they are upon something, while its reality is only what is said on the basis of conjecture and guesswork.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 117:

﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of who strays from His way, and He is most knowing of those who are guided.﴾ That is, He is most knowing of the two groups. "Man" (مَن, man) is either a relative pronoun or a qualifying noun, in a position of accusative (naṣb), governed by a verb implied by aʿlam (most knowing), not by aʿlam itself, since afʿal (the comparative form, "more/most") does not govern an explicit noun in such a construction. Or it is an interrogative (istifhamiyyah) in the nominative (marfūʿ), as the subject of the sentence (mubtadaʾ), with the predicate being "yuḍillu" (he leads astray), and the clause is suspended from the implied verb (muʿallaq ʿanhā al-fiʿl al-muqaddar). It has also been read as "man yaḍillu" (meaning: whom Allah leads astray), in which case "man" is in the accusative governed by the implied verb, or in the genitive by the annexation of aʿlam to it, meaning: the most knowing of those who lead astray, from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿whomever Allah leads astray﴾, or from "aḍlaltuhu" (I led him astray) when you find him astray. The superlative (tafḍīl) in knowledge refers to its abundance and its comprehensiveness regarding the aspects to which knowledge can attach, its necessity, and its being essential (bi-l-dhāt) rather than derived from another (bi-l-ghayr).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 118–119:

﴿So eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned﴾ is a consequence (musabbab) of the denunciation of following those who lead astray, who forbid what is lawful and make lawful what is forbidden. The meaning is: eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned at its slaughter, not of that over which the name of other than Him has been mentioned, or that which died of its own accord (hatf anfihi). ﴿If you are believers in His signs﴾, for belief in them requires permitting what God, glorified and exalted, has made lawful and avoiding what He has forbidden.

﴿And what reason do you have not to eat of that over which the name of God has been mentioned?﴾ That is, what purpose do you have in abstaining from eating it, and what prevents you from it?

﴿And He has already detailed for you what He has forbidden to you﴾, of what He has not forbidden, by His saying: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read fussila (with the verb in the passive form), while Nafi', Ya'qub and Hafs read harrama (with the verb in the active form). ﴿Except what you are compelled to﴾ of what He has forbidden to you, for it too is lawful in a state of necessity (darurah). ﴿And indeed, many lead astray﴾ by making lawful what is unlawful and forbidding what is lawful.

The Kufans read yudillun with a dammah on the ya', while the rest read it with a fathah. ﴿By their desires without knowledge﴾ by their conjecture, without any basis in evidence that yields knowledge. ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing of the transgressors﴾, those who exceed the truth into falsehood and the lawful into the unlawful.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 120–121:

﴿And leave alone the outward and the inward of sin.﴾ That is, what is openly done and what is done secretly; or what is done by the limbs and what is done by the heart. It is also said: fornication in the shops and taking secret lovers (akhdan). ﴿Indeed, those who earn sin will be recompensed for what they used to commit.﴾ Yaktasibuna: they acquire.

﴿And do not eat of that over which the name of God has not been mentioned.﴾ This is apparently a prohibition on eating an animal over which the name was left unmentioned, whether deliberately or through forgetfulness. Dawud took this view, and a similar position is reported from Ahmad. Malik and al-Shafi'i held the opposite, on the basis of his statement, may God's prayers and peace be upon him: "The slaughter of a Muslim is lawful even if the name of God has not been mentioned over it."

Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, distinguished between deliberate omission and forgetfulness, and interpreted the verse as referring to carrion, or to what was slaughtered with a name other than God's, on the basis of His words: ﴿And indeed it is an act of wickedness (fisq)﴾. Fisq refers to that over which a name other than God's has been invoked. The pronoun in "it" may refer to what is eaten, and it is also permissible that it refers to the act of eating which is indicated by "do not eat." ﴿And indeed the devils inspire﴾: they whisper. ﴿To their allies﴾: from among the disbelievers. ﴿To dispute with you﴾: by their saying, "You eat what you have killed yourselves, and your hunting animals, and you leave what God has killed." This supports the interpretation of carrion. ﴿And if you obey them﴾: in making lawful what He has forbidden. ﴿Indeed you are then polytheists﴾: for whoever abandons obedience to God Most High in favour of obedience to another and follows him in his religion has committed shirk. The omission of the fa' (the "then") here is acceptable because the conditional is in the past tense form.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 122:

﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people⦈ is an example for one whom Allah, glorified and exalted, has guided and rescued from misguidance, and has given the light of proofs and signs by which he reflects upon things, so that he distinguishes between truth and falsehood, and between the one who is upon the truth and the one who is upon falsehood.

Nafi' and Ya'qub read mayyitan (مَيْتًا) according to the original form (al-asl). ﴿Like one whose example is﴾ its description (ṣifatuhu), and it is a mubtada' (subject) whose khabar (predicate) is ﴿in the darknesses﴾. And His saying ﴿from which he is not coming out﴾ is a ḥal (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun hidden in the adverbial phrase (al-mustakinn fi al-ẓarf), not from the hā' in mathaluhu, for the sake of separation. It is an example for the one who remains upon misguidance and never departs from it in any state. ﴿Thus﴾ just as the faith of the believers was made attractive to them, ﴿so was made attractive to the disbelievers what they used to do﴾. The verse was revealed concerning Hamzah and Abu Jahl, and it was said concerning ʿUmar or ʿAmmar and Abu Jahl.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 123:

﴿And thus have We placed in every town its greatest criminals, that they may plot therein.﴾ That is: just as We placed in Makkah its greatest criminals, that they might plot therein, [so] We placed in every town its greatest criminals, that they might plot therein. "Ja'alna" (We placed) is used with the meaning of "sayyarna" (We made), and its two objects are "akabira mujrimiha" (its greatest criminals), with the second object placed before the first. Or [the phrase is] "fi kulli qaryatin akabira" (in every town, its greatest), and "mujrimiha" (its criminals) is an appositive (badal). It is also permissible for it to be a genitive complement (mudaf ilayhi) if "al-ja'l" (placing) is interpreted as "al-tamkin" (empowering). When the superlative form (af'al al-tafdil, elative) is put in a construct phrase (idafa), it may be either singular or agreeing in number, and for this reason it has been read as "akbara mujrimiha" (its greatest criminal, in the singular). The specification of "al-akabir" (the greatest) is because they are more capable of leading people astray and of plotting against them.

﴿And they plot only against themselves.﴾ Because its harm befalls them.

﴿And they do not perceive﴾ that.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 124:

﴿When a sign comes to them, they say, "We will never believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of Allah."﴾ This refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, according to what has been related: "Abu Jahl said, 'We have competed with the Banu Abd Manaf for nobility, until when we became like two racehorses running neck and neck, they said: "There is a prophet among us to whom revelation comes." By Allah, we will never accept him unless revelation comes to us just as it comes to him.'" Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Allah knows best where to place His message.﴾ This is a resumptive statement, answering them by pointing out that prophethood is not a matter of lineage or wealth, but of inner virtues which Allah, glorified and exalted be He, bestows upon whomever He wills among His servants. So He chooses for His messages whomever He knows to be fit for them, and He is most knowing of the place where He puts it. Ibn Kathir and Hafs, on the authority of Asim, read ﴿risalatahu﴾ (His message). ﴿Humiliation﴾ (saghar) means abasement and debasement ﴿before Allah﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, after their arrogance. It is also said that its implied sense is "from [the presence of] Allah." ﴿And a severe punishment﴾ ﴿for what they used to scheme﴾, meaning because of their scheming, or as a recompense for their scheming.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 125:

﴿Whomever Allah wills to guide﴾ — He makes him know the path of truth and grants him success in faith. ﴿He opens his breast to Islam﴾ — so it expands for it and He widens its space within him. This is a metaphor (kinaya) for making the self receptive to the truth, prepared for it to settle within it, purified of what would prevent or oppose it. The Most Excellent of Prayers and Peace (ﷺ) alluded to this when he was asked about it and said: "It is a light which Allah, glorified and exalted, casts into the heart of the believer, so it expands and widens for it."

They said: "Is there any sign by which it may be recognised?" He said: "Yes: turning in repentance (inabah) towards the abode of eternity, withdrawing from the abode of delusion (ghurur), and preparing for death before it descends." ﴿And whomever He wills to leave astray﴾ — ﴿He makes his breast constricted, tight﴾ — such that it recoils from accepting the truth, so faith does not enter it. Ibn Kathir read ḍayyiqan (ضَيْقًا) with lightening of the doubled letter, and Nafi' and Abu Bakr on the authority of ʿAsim read ḥarajan (حَرِجًا) with kasra, meaning intensely constricted; the rest read it with fatha, as a description using the verbal noun (masdar). ﴿As if he were climbing up into the sky﴾ — He likened him, as an exaggeration of the constriction of his breast, to one who attempts what he is unable to do, since climbing into the sky is a figure for what lies beyond ability. By this He alerted that faith is barred from him just as ascent is barred.

It is also said that its meaning is: as if he were ascending to the sky, recoiling from the truth and going far in fleeing from it. The original form of yaṣṣaʿʿadu (يَصَّعَّدُ) is yataṣaʿʿadu (يَتَصَعَّدُ), and it has been read that way. Ibn Kathir read yaṣṣaʿʿadu, and Abu Bakr on the authority of ʿAsim read yaṣṣāʿadu (يَصّاعَدُ), with the meaning of yataṣaʿʿadu. ﴿Thus﴾ — that is, just as his breast constricts and his heart remains far from the truth. ﴿Allah places defilement (rijs) upon those who do not believe﴾ — He places punishment or abandonment upon them. The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun for the purpose of giving the reason.

(p-182) ﴿Wa-hādhā﴾ ("And this") is a reference to the clear exposition that the Qur'an has brought, or to Islam, or to what preceded of divine success (tawfiq) and abandonment (khidhlan).

﴿Ṣirāṭu rabbika﴾ ("the path of your Lord") is the way that He has approved, or His custom and way which His wisdom requires. ﴿Mustaqīman﴾ ("straight") means without any crookedness; or [it means] just and consistent. It is a confirmative circumstantial phrase (ḥāl mu'akkidah), like His saying ﴿wa-huwa al-ḥaqq muṣaddiqan﴾ ("and it is the truth, confirming"); or it is a restrictive circumstantial phrase (ḥāl muqayyidah), and the governing element (al-'āmil) in it is the meaning of the demonstrative (al-ishārah). ﴿Qad faṣṣalnā al-āyāti li-qawmin yadhdhakkarūn﴾ ("We have indeed detailed the signs for a people who remember"), so that they know that the Capable One is Allah, glorified and exalted, and that everything that happens of good or evil is by His decree and creation, and that He is All-Knowing of the states of the servants, Wise and Just in what He does to them.

﴿Lahum dāru al-salām﴾ ("For them is the abode of peace"): the abode of Allah, He attributing Paradise to Himself as an honouring of it; or the abode of safety from what is hateful; or an abode in which their greeting is peace. ﴿'Inda rabbihim﴾ ("with their Lord") means under His guarantee, or it is a store laid up for them with Him, whose true nature none but Him knows. ﴿Wa-huwa waliyyuhum﴾ ("and He is their Walī") means their ally (muwālīhim), or their helper (nāṣiruhum). ﴿Bi-mā kānū ya'malūn﴾ ("because of what they used to do") means on account of their deeds; or [it means] He is their Mutawallī (the One who takes charge of them) with their recompense, so He takes charge of delivering it to them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 128:

"And [mention] the Day when He will gather them all together." It is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb: "remember" (udhkur) or "We will say" (naqul). The pronoun refers to those who will be gathered from the two weighty groups (al-thaqalan: humankind and jinn). Hafs, on the authority of ʿAsim, and Ruh, on the authority of Yaʿqub, read "yahshuruhum" with the letter ya' (third-person masculine).

﴿"O assembly of jinn"﴾ meaning the devils (al-shayatin).

﴿"You have indeed taken away much of mankind"﴾ that is, of their misguidance and leading astray; or, "from them," by making them your followers, so that they are gathered together with you, as in their saying: "The commander has taken much of the troops" (istakthara al-amir min al-junud).

﴿"And their allies from mankind will say"﴾ those who obeyed them.

﴿"Our Lord, some of us have enjoyed the benefit of others"﴾ meaning that humankind benefited from the jinn by pointing them to desires and to what leads to them, and the jinn benefited from humankind by their obedience and by attaining their aims. It has also been said that humankind's enjoyment of them was that they used to seek refuge with them in deserts and at times of fear, and their enjoyment of humankind was their acknowledgment that the jinn had power to grant them protection.

﴿"And we have reached our appointed term which You appointed for us"﴾ that is, the Resurrection. This is an acknowledgment of what they did of obeying Satan, following desire, denying the Resurrection, and a expression of regret over their state.

﴿"He will say: The Fire is your abode"﴾ your dwelling-place, or "its dwelling" (dhat mathwakum).

﴿"Abiding therein"﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal), and the governing element in it is "your abode" if it is taken as a verbal noun; and the sense of the genitive construction if it is taken as a place. ﴿"Except what God wills"﴾ except the times in which they will be moved from the Fire to the zamharir (the extreme cold). It has also been said that "except what God wills" refers to the period before entering, as if it were said: "The Fire is your abode forever, except for what He grants you respite."

﴿"Indeed your Lord is All-Wise"﴾ in His acts. ﴿"All-Knowing"﴾ of the deeds of the two weighty groups and their conditions.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 129–130:

﴿And thus We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others﴾: We leave some of them to others, or We make some of them rule over others, so that they lead them astray, or [We make them] companions and fellows of one another in the punishment, as they were in the world. ﴿Because of what they used to earn﴾: of disbelief and acts of disobedience.

﴿O assembly of jinn (unseen beings) and humans! Did not messengers from among you come to you?﴾ The messengers were from among humans only. However, since they were addressed together with the jinn, this is valid. A parallel to this is: ﴿From both of them come out pearls and coral﴾, and coral comes out of salt water, not fresh water. Some people held to the apparent meaning and said: messengers were sent to each of the two weighty creations (humans and jinn) from their own kind. It was also said: the messengers among the jinn were messengers of the messengers to them, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They returned to their people as warners﴾. ﴿They recount to you My verses and warn you of the meeting of this your day﴾, meaning the Day of Resurrection.

﴿They will say﴾ in reply: ﴿We bear witness against ourselves﴾ to [our] sin and disobedience. This is their acknowledgment of disbelief and of deserving the punishment.

(p-183) ﴿The worldly life deceived them, and they bore witness against themselves that they had been disbelievers﴾. This is a rebuke of them for their poor judgment and their error of opinion, for they were deceived by the worldly life and its defective pleasures, and turned away entirely from the Hereafter. The outcome of their affair was that they were compelled to testify against themselves to their disbelief and to submit to the everlasting punishment, as a warning to the listeners against being in a situation like theirs.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verse 131–132:

﴿That⦆ is a reference to the sending of the messengers, and it is the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada'), i.e., "the matter is that." ﴿That God would not destroy the cities unjustly while their people are unaware⦆ is a causal explanation (ta'lil) of the ruling. Here "an" (أنْ) is either a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah) or the lightened form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy "inna," meaning: the matter is that, due to the absence of your Lord being one who destroys the people of the cities for a wrong they committed, or because the situation is that your Lord would not destroy the people of the cities for a cause of wrongdoing they did, or while they are entangled in wrongdoing, or as wrongdoers while they are unaware, not having been warned by a messenger. Or it is a substitute (badal) for "that."

﴿And for each⦆ of those who are obligated (mukallafin), ﴿there are degrees⦆, i.e., ranks, ﴿according to what they did⦆ of their deeds, or according to their recompense, or for their sake. ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what they do⦆, so that no deed or the measure of what is deserved by it of reward or punishment would be hidden from Him. Ibn 'Amir read it with the "ta'" (تاء), giving precedence to address (khitab) over the third person (ghaybah).

﴿And for each⦆ of those who are obligated (mukallafin), ﴿there are degrees⦆, i.e., ranks, ﴿according to what they did⦆ of their deeds, or according to their recompense, or for their sake. ﴿And your Lord is not unaware of what they do⦆, so that no deed or the measure of what is deserved by it of reward or punishment would be hidden from Him. Ibn 'Amir read it with the "ta'" (تاء), giving precedence to address (khitab) over the third person (ghaybah).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 6, verses 133–134:

﴿And your Lord is the Self-Sufficient﴾ above His servants and their worship. ﴿Full of mercy﴾: He shows mercy to them by imposing obligations upon them, perfecting them, and He gives them respite despite their sins. In this there is an indication that what was mentioned before, namely the sending of messengers, is not for His benefit but out of His mercy towards His servants, and it lays the foundation for what follows, which is His saying: ﴿If He wills, He can remove you﴾, meaning: He has no need of you; if He wills, He can remove you, O disobedient ones. ﴿And make whom He wills succeed you﴾ of creation. ﴿As He produced you from the offspring of another people﴾, meaning: generation after generation; yet He has kept you alive out of mercy towards you.

﴿What you are promised﴾ of the Resurrection and its circumstances ﴿is surely coming﴾, that is, it will certainly occur without doubt. ﴿And you cannot escape﴾ Him, that is, you cannot elude Him who seeks you for it.
